docs.title: Flux
docs.text:
Flux searches for better designs and keeps only what it can prove. It makes designs with a script, a model or a coding agent, checks each one against your tests, measures the ones that pass with real tools, and decides from your objectives. It is built for hardware and software design-space exploration: RTL on an open 7 nm flow, Python and C code, cache prefetchers, or any program with settings to tune.

  • First loop

    A complete loop from an empty folder, in Python only: no model, no hardware tools.

    First loop →

  • Loop crafter

    Build the document in your browser, step by step, with the web app's own configurator.

    Loop crafter →

  • Write a loop with an agent

    Say what you want, give it your files, and let an agent write and check the loop.

    Write a loop with an agent →

docs.title: How a loop works
docs.text: A loop is a folder: a document, problem.yaml, and the scripts it names. Each pass, Flux chooses what to try, makes a design, runs your checks (a design that fails is never measured), runs the measurements cheapest first, and keeps the design that best meets your objectives. Every design, number and refusal goes on the record, so a run can stop and resume, and a result can be traced to what produced it.

docs.title: Configure
docs.text: Start with the working loop, copy a bundled example, or use flux new NAME. The document describes the experiment; the scripts beside it define how to generate, check, and measure a design. Use the Document reference for defaults and allowed values.

docs.title: Define the goal and interface
docs.text:
Write statement as the goal and contract as the interface and restrictions. State the function signature or module ports, supported inputs, numerical accuracy, and any implementation restrictions. Put executable checks in flow.test: prose alone does not establish correctness.

Choose the artifact language, such as python, systemverilog, or cpp. Flux uses it for the generated file extension. Say it: without it the design is a .txt file.

statement: Find a fast implementation of count_primes(n).
contract: >-
  Export count_primes(n). Return the number of primes strictly below n for
  nonnegative integer n. Do not change the interface or the benchmark.
language: python

docs.title: Choose how designs are made
docs.text:
Approach Configuration Use it when Script generate: {command: "..."} You can render each setting into a design FluxAgent generate: flux You want generated code or algorithms; this is the default Coding agent generate: claude (also codex, opencode) The design needs edits across files or interactive checks Fixed candidates generate: {catalog: [...]} You already have artifacts to compare Tune settings A search space, with no generator command Commands consume the chosen settings directly

A script generator writes {artifact}; its stdout is not the artifact. For example:

flow:
  generate:
    command: ["{python}", "{home}/render.py", "{artifact}", "{block}"]

The search supplies {block}. Use {point} when the generator needs the entire point as a JSON file, or {params} for settings shared by your own commands. See Search and agents for the search and agent setup.

Commands accept a string or a list of arguments. A string is split into arguments, rather than executed by a shell: if you need a pipeline, put it in a script or explicitly use bash -c. Prefer argument lists when paths or values contain spaces. A command beginning with flux uses the same Flux installation as the loop.

docs.title: Build a gate, cheapest check first
docs.text:
Checks run in the order written. The first failure refuses the candidate and later checks do not run. Name them for the action they perform:

flow:
  test:
    build: "{python} -m py_compile {artifact}"
    correctness:
      run: "{python} {home}/check.py {artifact}"
      timeout_s: 120

A check named build treats every nonzero exit as a build failure. Any check exiting 3 also means the candidate did not build. Other checks use the default N failing pattern when it is present; otherwise exit 0 passes and a nonzero exit counts as one failure. Debug output on stderr is retained and is not, by itself, a failure.

For a checker with a different output format, specify the pattern deliberately:

flow:
  test:
    tests:
      run: "{python} {home}/check.py {artifact}"
      count_re: 'failures=(\d+)'

count_re captures an integer failure count. fail_re counts matching failures instead. These patterns scan stdout and stderr; a match can report failure even when the process exits 0. Keep debug messages distinct from your machine-readable test summary.

For RTL, define the ports and reference function in golden.py, then use:

flow:
  test:
    lint: "fluxpreset rtl lint {artifact}"
    golden: "fluxpreset golden {artifact} --golden {home}/golden.py"

The golden model describes vectors, clocked designs, and floating-point tolerances. flux tools lists the built-in checks and their commands, and the configurator offers them as a check's Type or a measurement's Tool under Flux presets.

docs.title: Measure surviving designs
docs.text:
Measurements run stage by stage in document order. Start with a cheap screen and put the costliest measurement last. A custom stage must print the metrics it declares:

flow:
  measure:
    screen:
      command: "{python} {home}/bench.py {artifact} --quick"
      metrics: [time_ms, bytes]
      cutoff: {metric: bytes, below: 4096}
    confirm:
      command: "{python} {home}/bench.py {artifact} --full"
      metrics: [time_ms, bytes]
      timeout_s: 1800
  select: {finalists: 2}

The --quick and --full flags here are flags your benchmark must implement. It should print, for example, time_ms=2.31 bytes=2048. Metrics can appear on stdout or stderr; a nonzero measurement command exit rejects its numbers. Use metrics_re for a different output format.

Every stage must declare the metrics required by its objectives. The command belongs to the application, or is one of Flux's presets (fluxpreset rtl measure ...; see Presets). Declare the tools it requires too:

flow:
  measure:
    screen:
      command: "fluxpreset rtl measure {artifact} --stage synth --clock-ps 1000"
      metrics: [fmax_mhz, area_um2, power_w, cell_count]
      needs: [yosys, openroad]
    confirm:
      command: "fluxpreset rtl measure {artifact} --stage place --clock-ps 1000"
      metrics: [fmax_mhz, area_um2, power_w, cell_count]
      needs: [yosys, openroad]
      timeout_s: 1800
  select: {finalists: 2}

needs: [tool_name] declares required executables for a custom stage. A stage is skipped when a declared tool is missing; check the reported stage before treating a screening number as a confirmed result. --screen-only omits the costliest stage of a multi-stage chain.

docs.title: Cutoffs and estimates
docs.text:
cutoff decides whether a measured design proceeds: at is a minimum, below is a maximum, and within retains a fraction of the best result for that metric. A list requires every condition to pass:

cutoff:
  - {metric: fmax_mhz, at: 1000}
  - {metric: area_um2, below: 80}

An optional estimate can screen a design before paying for the tool:

estimate: {kind: surrogate, margin: 0.05}

The surrogate uses prior measurements at that stage and needs at least three rows. An estimate outside a cutoff or objective limit by more than the margin skips that stage. Estimates are not measurements; enable this only when that screening trade-off fits your experiment. The reference also covers command and model estimators.

docs.title: Define what wins
docs.text:
Separate limits (objectives with goal) from preferences (objectives without one):

objectives:
  - {metric: fmax_mhz, direction: maximize, goal: 1000}
  - {metric: area_um2, direction: minimize, goal: 80}
  - {metric: power_w, direction: minimize}

This asks for at least 1000 MHz, at most 80 µm², then minimum power among feasible designs. Goal-less preferences are compared in their written order. An absolute goal uses the deepest stage unless its stage names another. If nothing meets every limit, the report describes the closest standing design and its shortfall; it does not produce a feasible decision artifact.

Use balance: true on multiple goal-less objectives for a compromise at the frontier's knee. A relative limit such as {metric: speedup, direction: maximize, keep: 0.9, above: 1.0} keeps 90% of the best measured gain over the baseline, instead of specifying an absolute goal.

docs.title: Control time and concurrency
docs.text:
budget:
  passes: 10
  steps: 3
  repair_attempts: 6
  batch: 1
  workers: 1
  parallel: 1

passes bounds the whole run; steps bounds work within one pass. repair_attempts bounds attempts to fix a draft. batch is designs from a search within a pass, workers controls measurement concurrency, and parallel controls simultaneous passes. They are separate knobs. On a server, an administrator must allow parallel work for the app; otherwise its concurrency cap wins. In the configurator, parallel, workers and (for a loop with parts) parallel_parts are Extra › Running, which also says whether the admin allows the loop parallel work and links to its Settings › Preferences › Advanced. Keep timed benchmarks isolated, including from parallel passes and overlapping part work. The budget reference includes those settings.

Omit passes, or use 0, to run until manually stopped. Finding a feasible design or a stalled search does not end an unlimited run. Individual attempts still have their budgets and timeouts; Run, stop, resume explains stopping and resuming.

docs.title: Add context and reusable settings
docs.text:
params: {input_size: 1000000, repetitions: 9}
flow:
  knowledge:
    files: [spec.md, reference.py]
    hidden: [check.py]

params reaches scripts through the {params} JSON file. knowledge.files reach every model prompt and agent brief; knowledge.hidden keeps the gate's files from the agents. Knowledge, skills, hidden paths covers what agents read and what they may not.

Check each edited document with flux task check FOLDER, then do a bounded run with flux task run FOLDER --passes 1. Continue with Search and agents or look up the remaining fields in the Document reference.

docs.title: Tune a program's settings
docs.text:
statement: The fastest block size and thread count for my kernel.
flow:
  orchestrate:
    space:
      block: [16, 32, 64, 128, 256]
      threads: [1, 2, 4, 8]
  test: "{python} {home}/check.py {block} {threads}"
  measure:
    bench:
      command: "{home}/run.sh --block {block} --threads {threads}"
      metrics: [time_ms]
objectives: [{metric: time_ms, direction: minimize}]
budget: {workers: 1}
  • Time alone. Set budget.workers: 1, and pin the program's own threads if it has any. Measured side by side, runs disturb each other: a block size can look many times better than it is.
  • Keep the gate even when correctness seems obvious: a setting that crashes or returns the wrong answer is refused before it is timed.
  • A knob is any placeholder: {block} works in any command, and in a generator script.

docs.title: Choose a search for the space
Trade-offs and limits
docs.text:
• One limit, then the rest: a goal on the first objective, then the next decides among the designs that meet it: "the smallest that makes 1 GHz".
  • A true trade-off: two objectives without a goal and the pareto policy. The report shows the front; balance: true picks its knee.
  • A hard limit on a cost: make it a check (refuse what exceeds it), a stage cutoff, or a policy floor ({metric: storage_bytes, at: 98304}).

docs.title: When a model writes the designs
docs.text:
• It gets it wrong a lot: give it the facts in flow.knowledge (a spec, reference code, a method note) and skills. flux log RECORD shows what it was told and what it said.
  • Numeric hardware (floating point, transcendentals, fixed point): use a golden model and budget.prototype: true. The model proves the algorithm in Python on every input first, and the loop spells it as RTL. A prototype too costly to be worth synthesising (budget.prototype_cost_max) is made cheaper before anything is built.
  • A coding agent instead: flow.generate: claude (or codex, opencode). It writes in its own folder; the loop runs the gate and brings a failure back to the same session. With a prototype stage, it writes the prototype, which suits hard numeric functions better than asking for RTL directly.
  • Let it run: a run goes on until you stop it, and each start resumes from the record. When nothing is left to try, it explores for a better design.
  • Steer it: a note typed in the TUI (f), or in the loop's Chat in the web app, reaches the next prompt.

docs.title: Read the results
docs.text:
• flux task run FOLDER --json answer.json: the decision, the front and the refusals as JSON.
  • flux report RECORD: an HTML report with the front, the best so far over time, and every design.
  • flux log RECORD: every model and agent turn, for when a run did not go as you expected.

docs.title: Knowledge, skills, hidden paths
docs.text: What the model and the agents read besides the document, and what they may not read. The fields are in the Document reference.

docs.title: Files, notes and papers
docs.text:
flow:
  knowledge:
    files: [spec.md, reference.py]
    text: Prefer implementations that are easy to maintain.
    digest: claude
    lessons: mined
  • files and text reach every prompt and brief: a spec, reference code, a method note. A folder counts as each of its files; PDFs are read as text.
  • The library: the loop's library/ folder holds papers and notes; each project's library it is linked into appears inside it, read-only, at library/<project>@<group>/. digest says who summarises them (flux, FluxAgent, or an agent). Agents read it with flux library (below).
  • lessons: mined reuses lessons drawn from the loop's record; an agent's name has that agent draw them.

  • knowledge: off turns all reading off.

  • A project's knowledge (web app, a project's Knowledge tab): entries its people keep, each one insight under one of the project's topics, proven by designs of its loops -- added by hand, or proposed by Flux's collector once a linked loop's top designs have mostly changed (one call to the loop's own model, outside the loop; curators accept or reject each proposal; see the collector). A loop linked into the project reads its accepted entries (never a proposal) with flux knowledge: flux knowledge lists each project's topics with their questions and its entries' headlines, flux knowledge search "<words>" [--topic t] [--project p] gives the matching entries whole (headline, analysis, designs: loop · design · rank), flux knowledge show <id> one; --json for data. A coding agent's brief carries one line per project that has an accepted entry -- Project knowledge: silicon@hw-lab — pipelining 2 · timing 1. Query it before choosing a design direction, as your first command, e.g. flux knowledge search "<words>" … --; a plain model step, which runs no command, is not told. The entries are those of the loop's start (a change reaches the next start; the run's log says the version it read). A loop in no project, whose projects have no accepted entry or whose knowledge is off is told nothing; see Groups › Knowledge.

A model that keeps getting a design wrong usually lacks a fact, not effort: a method note with the method and the facts (not a design) helps more than more passes.

docs.title: Reading the library: flux library
docs.text:
A coding agent reads the library -- the loop's own and every project library it reads -- in pieces, never a whole PDF at once:

flux library                               # every document, one line each: name · pages or lines · what it is
flux library "QUERY" [--n 5]               # the nearest documents, each with its digest and its 3 best passages
flux library digest  PAPER                 # its digest
flux library outline PAPER                 # its sections, each with its pages and lines
flux library read    PAPER --section 3.2   # one section
flux library read    PAPER --around "QUERY"  # the passages that match best, with a little context
flux library read    PAPER --lines 120-220 # or --pages 3-4 for a PDF; --from 221 goes on from a line
  • Names. A document is named by its place in library/: booth.md, papers/x.pdf, silicon@hw-lab/x.pdf for a project's (library/silicon@hw-lab/x.pdf and a file name or stem one document has are accepted too).
  • Outline. From its headings: Markdown #, LaTeX \section, a PDF's numbered headings (3.2 Method) and the usual unnumbered ones (Abstract, References ...). A document with none is cut by its pages (a PDF) or in chunks of 120 lines.
  • Capped. Every answer prints about 3000 tokens at most; a cut one ends with the exact command that continues (… continue: flux library read x.pdf --from 221). Every passage says where it is: section, page, lines.
  • Search. The library's own BM25 ranking, offline and the same every time. A PDF's text (pdftotext) is cached by its content ($XDG_CACHE_HOME/flux/text), so its line numbers stay the same.
  • Hidden. A path the loop or a project hides from its agents is refused.
  • Inside an agent's turn it reads that turn's loop (in the sandbox too); elsewhere --loop or the current folder. Plain text; --json for data. A coding agent's LIBRARY section names these commands and asks for a first step (flux library "<your method or bottleneck>", then flux library read PAPER --around "QUERY": a digest is a summary, not the method); a loop with no library and no project library is told of no papers. The old flux loop library and flux loop digest answer as they did.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md: front matter with name and description, then the instructions, and any files they use. Put skills in the loop's skills/ folder and they are read without a word in the document. The model gets an index and a skill tool; every coding agent of the loop finds them in its work folder. The built-in flux-loop-commands skill (how to read the loop's record with flux loop ...) comes with them.

skills: [skills, ../shared-skills]           # these folders instead of skills/
skills: {"off": [flux-loop-commands]}        # skills/ and the built-in one, this one off
skills: "off"                                # none at all

--skill DIR on flux task run or flux ask adds a folder for one run.

docs.title: Hidden from AI
docs.text:
A gate is only as good as the agent's ignorance of it. An agent that can read the tests can write a design that passes them and nothing else. knowledge.hidden names paths no agent and no prompt may read:

flow:
  knowledge:
    hidden: [tests/, golden.py, "params/*.json"]

The loop's own checks, measurements and scripts read these paths as ever, and a check's failure text still reaches the agent. Paths are relative to the loop's folder; sub-loops hide their parent's paths too. An agent's own hidden: option adds paths for that agent alone.

Each agent's brief names them as off limits, and its permission settings refuse reading and editing them where the agent has per-path rules (Claude Code and OpenCode; Codex has only the brief). Nothing more is taken away: the agent keeps its search tools and its shell, and a command that names a hidden path (pytest tests) is not refused. Hidden is trust plus each agent's own deny rules, no sandbox: a search or a script the agent writes could still read a file, so for secrets, rely on the sandbox. Parameters lists each agent's rules.

In the web app, hide a path:

  • in Files, from a file's or folder's Actions › Hide from AI;
  • in the configurator's Graph, on the Knowledge box;
  • when adding files to New loop › Agent, with Hide from AI on the file;
  • with flux ask --hidden PATH on the command line.

docs.title: Ideas cleanup
docs.text:
The loop keeps an ideas notebook: each hypothesis a model or agent proposed, with the designs that tested it. Over many passes it fills with the same idea in other words. knowledge.ideas has it cleaned up in a pass's Setup, once it has grown:

flow:
  knowledge:
    lessons: mined
    ideas: flux                          # FluxAgent; or an agent: claude; or {by: flux, open: 30, new: 15}
  • When: before a pass, if the notebook holds at least open open ideas (20 by default) and new of them came since the last cleanup (10). Otherwise the step is a note in Live (Setup · tidy ideas, "14 open ideas, 3 new since the last cleanup") and no model is asked.
  • What: one short call (or one turn of the agent) reads each open idea's title, hypothesis and evidence and answers which ideas are the same. Each group becomes one idea: the others are merged into it, keep their text and evaluations, and their evidence counts under the kept idea. Nothing is deleted. A design that names a merged idea, and a queued one, tests the kept idea. The same call ranks the open ideas, the most promising first, each with a reason: Results › Ideas lists them in that order. The ranking is only for you to read: the loop's own choice of ideas never reads it.
  • Undo: flux loop ideas --unmerge 7 makes idea 7 its own idea again (idea 7, #7 and the idea's id say it too); naming a kept idea undoes every merge into it. flux loop ideas shows each idea's number and its merges. An idea is said by its number as "idea 7", never "#7", which is a design's.

Unsaid, the cleanup is off. ideas: off says so. In the web app it is Ideas cleanup in the Graph's Knowledge box, beside the lessons.

docs.title: Workbench
docs.text: workbench/ beside the document is the agents' own folder: tools they build and notes they keep, shared by the loop's agents and kept across runs. knowledge.workbench says who sums it up for the next prompt when it changed (off, flux, or an agent); by default, whoever digests the papers. In the web app it is Files › Workbench; the library and its digests are Files › Library.

docs.title: Loop crafter
docs.text:
The web app's own configurator, running in this page: build a loop's problem.yaml step by step, with the document beside each step. Nothing leaves your browser; Download problem.yaml, save it in your loop's folder with the scripts it names, then run flux task check FOLDER.

The loop crafter needs JavaScript. Without it, build your own loop walks through the same file by hand.

docs.text:

docs.title: Search and agents
docs.text:
A loop separates what to try next (flow.orchestrate) from how to make the design (flow.generate). The gate and measurement stages establish the results. You can change the search or generator while keeping those checks, measurements, and objectives.

The configurator's Graph draws the loop as a ring: Search (orchestrate) chooses what to try, Design (generate) makes it, Check (test) and Measure (measure) establish the facts, and Choose (select) decides. A failed check goes back to Design. The setup boxes beside the ring run before the passes or feed every prompt.

docs.title: Search a space of settings
docs.text:
Use a finite space when you can list meaningful choices. The generator and other commands receive those choices as placeholders:

flow:
  orchestrate:
    policy: sweep
    space:
      algorithm: [list_sieve, slice_sieve, odd_sieve]
      wheel: [0, 1]
    seeds:
      - {algorithm: list_sieve, wheel: 0}
  generate: {command: "{python} {home}/render.py {artifact} {algorithm} {wheel}"}

The seed is measured first; an omitted knob uses its first choice. The first seed is the home point. Order numeric choices meaningfully because local search uses that order.

Policy How it chooses experiments sweep Enumerate distinct combinations; a useful baseline for a small space montecarlo Sample distinct random points gradient Follow measured improvements among nearby choices anneal Make local moves and sometimes accept worse points to escape a region genetic Evolve a population through selection and mutation pareto Explore trade-offs; requires at least two objectives flux or model Ask FluxAgent to propose legal points from the space and measured history (model: its old name) control Compare the home point with only some of the incumbent's knobs kept (keep: [...]) phases Run several of these in order, each with its own options command Your own search script: orchestrate: {command: "...", timeout_s: 600} (contract)

One pass normally carries one point. budget.batch lets it carry several; budget.parallel runs several passes simultaneously. A policy finishing its finite walk does not, by itself, stop an unlimited run. Use a pass cap for a bounded sweep.

Passes running at once share the Setup steps that read only what every pass reads: the model's reading of the document, the division into parts, the papers' digest, the workbench's README, the ideas cleanup and the agent's lessons. The first pass of a wave to reach such a step runs it; the others wait and take its result, and their step says "shared with pass N". A step that fails the way a pass alone goes on from (a digest or a cleanup that could not run) is that result for the whole wave, and the next wave asks again; a step that raises is tried again by one waiting pass, not by all of them. The gates, opening the record and preparing the inputs stay each pass's own. One pass at a time runs every step in every pass, as before.

Configure a policy's own options under its name:

flow:
  orchestrate:
    policy:
      gradient: {steps: 16, patience: 2, reach: adjacent}
    space:
      block: [16, 32, 64, 128]
      order: [ijk, ikj, jki]

The search reference lists policy options and defaults. For a multi-phase search, keep the space and put a phases policy around its ordered phases:

flow:
  orchestrate:
    space: {block: [16, 32, 64, 128], order: [ijk, ikj, jki]}
    policy:
      phases:
        phases:
          - {policy: montecarlo, name: sample, samples: 8, seed: 0}
          - {policy: gradient, name: tune, knobs: [block], steps: 8}

docs.title: Conditional choices and components
docs.text:
Avoid measuring a knob that has no effect on a chosen algorithm:

space:
  algorithm: [list_sieve, slice_sieve, odd_sieve]
  wheel: {values: [0, 1], when: {algorithm: [list_sieve]}}

This is the space inside flow.orchestrate. Inactive choices sit at their home values and are not repeatedly measured as different designs. A nested component groups its knobs:

space:
  prefetch:
    optional: true
    distance: [1, 2, 4]
    degree: [1, 2]

The search sees prefetch.on, prefetch.distance, and prefetch.degree. {point} provides these as nested JSON to a generator. A choice can also use from: "out/invented/*.sv" beside values to include filenames discovered when the document loads.

docs.title: Let a model or agent explore designs
docs.text:
A model or agent can invent algorithms and architectures without a predefined knob space. The default guidance is adaptive: reasoned risks are welcome, and exploration can happen before the incumbent stalls. Say who decides what to try next, and with which emphasis, in flow.orchestrate; who writes the code is flow.generate, set apart:

flow:
  orchestrate: {by: claude, dse: adaptive}
  generate: claude
budget:
  exploration_quota: 0.25
flow.orchestrate.dse Emphasis adaptive Choose local improvements or a new approach from the evidence explore Try materially different algorithms, architectures, or representations improve Improve the objectives through local or structural changes tune Favor parameter and implementation changes near promising designs finetune Favor small changes whose effect can be attributed variations Develop distinct versions of promising approaches sweep, montecarlo, anneal, gradient, genetic, pareto Apply the corresponding search emphasis to reasoning and prompts

Here dse is prompt and choice guidance, not a hard ban on broader changes. It is distinct from policy, which selects an actual search algorithm over a space. Prefer policy: sweep for enumerating knob combinations; use {by: claude, dse: explore} to guide an agent's work. The algorithm names all have implemented walks: gradient is coordinate descent over discrete choices, rather than derivatives; pareto uses a tree guided by trade-offs across the first two objectives. Without a space, these names guide the reasoning instead of running those walks. Preferences influence choices but do not force every experiment to follow them, and a script that writes a design does not read model prompts.

In the configurator, the whole search is the Search box on the Graph: a Kind, then a Policy, then the Settings to search (each a name and its values); Extra only names it.

exploration_quota reserves a minimum share of recorded search choices for exploration, including across parallel passes. It counts attempts, not elapsed seconds, successful designs, or a guaranteed fraction of a finite grid. Use 0 for no enforced quota. Existing verified candidates remain available when an experiment is worse or fails. Correctness checks and the contract still apply to every new design.

Guidance reaches initial generation, repairs, prototype work, and later improvements. Logs record the selected move and its reason. A finite budget or manual stop controls the run; reaching a goal or keeping the same incumbent does not stop an unlimited run.

docs.title: Put agents in the right steps
docs.text:
Name an installed agent directly, and use {by: ..., ...} only when adding options:

flow:
  validate: rules
  orchestrate: {by: claude, dse: adaptive}
  plan: {by: claude, session: pass}
  generate: {by: claude, timeout_s: 1800, probe: {gate: 20, stages: 3}}
  select: {by: claude, finalists: 2}
  knowledge: {digest: claude, lessons: mined}

claude, codex, and opencode are built in; a server can offer additional named agents. They can plan, generate, and advise decisions. flow.test and flow.measure remain commands: an agent cannot replace their factual results. Selection still uses the objectives; an agent's advice is checked and can fall back to the rules.

A critic is a second opinion on one box: critic: under orchestrate (the split or the direction), test (a design the checks passed), measure (a stage's numbers) or select (the pick). It is flux (FluxAgent), an agent, or {by: ..., rounds: N}. A rejection is a verdict: the design fails, the numbers are marked, or the pick is made again without it.

flow:
  test:
    correctness: "{python} {home}/check.py {artifact}"
    critic: claude
  select: {finalists: 2, critic: {by: flux, rounds: 2}}

See critics for each box's rules.

A generation agent resumes one session for a part through its repairs until that part is admitted; a later improvement starts fresh. Do not set session on generate. Decision steps such as plan and a critic accept session: turn (default) or session: pass.

Agents can use flux probe to check their current file during a turn. probe budgets those checks per turn. Direct use of certain raw tools is restricted by default; allow can give specific tools back when that suits the task. See agent options.

For FluxAgent, use orchestrate: {by: flux, dse: adaptive} and generate: flux (model, its old name, is the same). Models and agents explains endpoint and agent setup.

docs.title: Split a larger design
docs.text: A design too large for one piece can be split into parts, or into sub-loops whose decided designs a parent composes: see Split a larger design.

docs.title: Models and agents
docs.text:
Flux talks to two kinds of AI, configured apart:

  • FluxAgent (flux in a document, a chat or --author; model, its old name, is the same): Flux's own model, on any OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint, for the loop's own calls (proposing points, writing designs with generate: flux, reviewing, digesting papers).
  • Coding agents: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or one a server adds. Each runs on its own endpoint, model and login, never on FluxAgent.

A loop whose designs come from a script, with no flux or agent in its flow, needs neither. flux selftest says which model and endpoint a run would use, and whether each agent is ready.

docs.title: FluxAgent
docs.text:
By default Flux asks a local Ollama (OLLAMA_BASE_URL, the model in FLUX_LLM_MODEL). A remote OpenAI-compatible endpoint (LocalAI, vLLM, llama.cpp's server, a hosted service) uses:

export FLUX_REMOTE_BASE_URL=https://your-model-server.example/v1
export FLUX_REMOTE_MODEL=your-model-name
export FLUX_REMOTE_API_KEY=your-key          # only if the endpoint checks keys
flux selftest
Variable What it does FLUX_LLM_MODEL The local model's name OLLAMA_BASE_URL The local server's root FLUX_REMOTE_BASE_URL An endpoint of your own; setting it switches to it FLUX_REMOTE_MODEL The model's name on that endpoint FLUX_REMOTE_API_KEY, FLUX_REMOTE_API_KEY_FILE Its key, or a file whose first line is the key FLUX_LLM_REMOTE 1 forces the remote endpoint, 0 the local one FLUX_LLM_TIMEOUT_S Seconds one request may take; raise it for slow servers and long turns FLUX_LLM_STREAM 0 turns streaming off, for proxies that break it

--model NAME on flux task run and flux ask overrides the model for one run. If a service refuses the structured output Flux asks for, try --no-structured.

docs.title: Settings that last
docs.text:
Every flux command reads ~/.config/flux/flux.env (or the file FLUX_CONFIG names): NAME=value lines, used only where the shell did not set the variable. Keep the key in its own file (mode 600) rather than in flux.env:

FLUX_REMOTE_BASE_URL=https://your-model-server.example/v1
FLUX_REMOTE_MODEL=your-model-name
FLUX_REMOTE_API_KEY_FILE=~/.config/flux/server.key

Keep keys in the environment or the web app's settings, never in a loop's document.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text:
Ollama on this machine:

ollama pull qwen3:4b                  # any tag; then
export FLUX_LLM_MODEL=qwen3:4b
flux task run flux/applications/primes --passes 1     # from the repository root

A large model on a CPU takes minutes per turn; use a GPU, or a smaller model for small problems. For an Ollama on another machine, set OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://HOST:11434.

A server of your own (LocalAI, vLLM, llama.cpp's server): set FLUX_REMOTE_BASE_URL, FLUX_REMOTE_MODEL and, if it checks keys, FLUX_REMOTE_API_KEY, as above. Raise FLUX_LLM_TIMEOUT_S (for example to 1800) for long turns with tools.

OpenRouter: FLUX_LLM_REMOTE=1, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and FLUX_REMOTE_MODEL set to an OpenRouter model id. With FLUX_LLM_REMOTE=1 and no FLUX_REMOTE_BASE_URL, Flux asks OpenRouter.

OpenCode on a server of your own: in OpenCode's configuration (~/.config/opencode/opencode.json), read the key as "apiKey": "{env:FLUX_AGENT_API_KEY}" and set FLUX_OPENCODE_API_KEY (in flux.env, or OpenCode's card in the web app). Tell OpenCode the model's real limits, and keep a thinking model's reasoning short, or it can end turn after turn on an empty reply:

"models": {"MODEL": {"limit": {"context": 58112, "output": 16384},
                     "options": {"reasoningEffort": "low"}}}

and "timeout": 1800000 in the provider's options. OpenCode's own prompt and tools take about 10,000 tokens of the window.

docs.title: Coding agents
docs.text:
An agent must be installed and logged in where Flux runs (inside the sandbox, with its own home: flux login --home ... -- claude /login, or the web app's Account › Agents). Flux's Nix development shell carries Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode (from nixchip), and Flux finds them on PATH; nothing else to install. To run another copy, a newer one say, set FLUX_<NAME>_BIN to its program: it wins while it names a runnable file, and Flux falls back to the PATH's when it does not (an editor extension's binary that an update moved). Check one with:

flux agent test claude          # its program and login
flux agent test claude --live   # also one short question
Variable What it does FLUX_<NAME>_BIN The agent's program, e.g. FLUX_CLAUDE_BIN, FLUX_CODEX_BIN, FLUX_OPENCODE_BIN FLUX_<NAME>_ARGS Extra arguments, added before the prompt FLUX_<NAME>_BASE_URL, FLUX_<NAME>_MODEL, FLUX_<NAME>_API_KEY The agent's own endpoint, model and key FLUX_<NAME>_OAUTH_TOKEN A login token, for agents that take one FLUX_<NAME>_TIMEOUT_S Seconds per turn (default 1800); a document's timeout_s wins

None of FLUX_REMOTE_*, FLUX_LLM_* or OPENROUTER_API_KEY reaches an agent's turn. Without settings of its own, an agent runs on its own configuration file and login. In the web app, each agent's card says "not configured" when it has neither.

An agent writes; it does not compile, simulate or test. The loop runs the checks and measurements, and the agent checks its file mid-turn with flux probe, within a budget. See Agent options for probe, allow, timeout_s and the rest.

docs.title: Which model for which problem
docs.text:
The loop does not make a weak model strong: it keeps what passes, refuses what does not, and turns each failure into the next prompt. In this project's runs, a mid-size model wrote a correct Python loop or a small adder on its first draft, but hard numeric hardware (a floating-point function within 1 ULP) needed more than RTL from a plain prompt. What helped:

  • a prototype stage (budget.prototype: true with a golden model): the algorithm proven in Python on every input, then spelled as RTL by the loop;
  • a method note in flow.knowledge: the method and the facts, not a design;
  • a coding agent writing the prototype, told by the loop where it fails.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
• No answer: a run that needs a model asks its endpoint first and stops before the first pass when it does not answer, refuses the key, or lacks the model. flux task check shows the same line.
  • Start with the log: flux log RECORD shows every model and agent turn: the prompt, the reply, the tool calls, and the error.
  • Timeouts: raise FLUX_LLM_TIMEOUT_S for the model, timeout_s for an agent.
  • Context: an agent that outgrows its endpoint's context window continues in a fresh session; raise the window if you can.

docs.title: Document
docs.text:
Everything a loop's document, problem.yaml, can say, and the contract every command it names must follow: arguments, placeholders, what to print, exit codes. It is written from the code and checked against it.

Use Configure for why you would choose each setting, flux task check FOLDER to validate a document, and flux task migrate FOLDER --write to upgrade an older one.

docs.title: The document at a glance
docs.text:
Only statement is required. A complete document; the numbered marks say where each part is described:

statement: Count the primes below n, as fast as possible.  # (1)!
contract: >-  # (2)!
  A Python module defining count_primes(n) that returns
  exactly how many primes are below n.
language: python

flow:  # (3)!
  orchestrate:
    policy: sweep
    space: {method: [trial_division, sieve, slice_sieve]}
  generate:
    command: "{python} {home}/render.py {artifact} {method}"
  test:  # (4)!
    build: "{python} -m py_compile {artifact}"
    correctness:
      run: "{python} {home}/check.py {artifact}"
      timeout_s: 60
  measure:  # (5)!
    quick:
      command: "{python} {home}/bench.py {artifact} 50000"
      metrics: [time_ms]
      cutoff: {metric: time_ms, below: 20}
    full:
      command: "{python} {home}/bench.py {artifact} 1000000"
      metrics: [time_ms]
  select: {finalists: 2}

objectives:  # (6)!
  - {metric: time_ms, direction: minimize, goal: 20}

budget: {passes: 5, workers: 1}  # (7)!
params: {n_max: 1000000}  # (8)!
  1. What to make. The only required field.
  2. Rules every design must follow: names, ports, what is forbidden.
  3. Who does each box of the loop: here a search over three methods, and a script that writes each design (flow settings).
  4. The checks, in order; the first that fails refuses the design (check settings).
  5. The measurements, cheapest first. cutoff decides which designs go on to the next stage; select.finalists how many climb (measurement settings).
  6. What decides. A goal makes an objective a limit: here at most 20 ms (objectives).
  7. How much to spend (budget).
  8. Your own settings, handed to every command as the {params} file.

docs.title: Files and loading
docs.text:
• The folder is the loop. Its name is the loop's id: 1 to 60 letters, digits, _ and -. There is no id key; saying one is refused.
  • The document is problem.yaml (or problem.yml, problem.json). Alternates beside it are NAME.problem.yaml; each has its own record, out/<id>.NAME.db.
  • Beside it: your scripts, library/ (papers and notes the model reads), workbench/ (the agents' own tools and notes, kept across runs), skills/ (read unless skills: says otherwise), and out/ (the record, the cache and the decided design, written by Flux).
  • Parsing: a YAML or JSON error reports its line and column; a document that is not a mapping is refused. Unknown keys are refused with a "did you mean" hint.
  • Older documents are never upgraded silently: flux task migrate FOLDER shows what changes and --write saves it.
  • Normal form: equivalent spellings (plan: flux and plan: {by: flux}) load to the same document and share one record -- model, FluxAgent's old name, too.

docs.title: Document fields
docs.text:
Field Values / default Purpose statement Required non-empty string What to build or optimize contract String; empty Interface and rules every design must follow (names, ports, what is forbidden) language String; inferred, else text The design's file type (table below) flow Map; defaults below Who does each step: search, generation, checks, measurements, and the supporting boxes objectives List; empty Limits and ordered preferences (objectives) budget Map; defaults below Run length, repairs, concurrency, prototypes (budget) params Map; empty Your own settings, handed to any command as the {params} JSON file parts List of names, map of descriptions, or decompose Pieces of one artifact (parts) subtasks List of folders or inline documents, or decompose Child problems, each its own loop (sub-loops) max_subtasks Integer; 4 Most children when subtasks: decompose skills off, a folder or list of folders, or {from, off}; skills/ Skills (a folder with SKILL.md) the model and agents can load (skills) ladder true, false, or a map; absent The part improvement ladder (ladder) baseline true, false, or a map; absent A reference measured before pass 1 (baseline)

language sets the design file's extension, matched without case:

Language Extension Language Extension systemverilog .sv cpp, c++ .cpp verilog .v c .c vhdl .vhd cuda .cu python .py opencl .cl text .txt rust .rs yaml .yaml markdown .md json .json shell, bash .sh chisel, scala .scala anything else . + the name, lower case, no spaces

When language is absent it is inferred only from a check or stage that starts with a built-in tool's full command (in practice the Verilator lint line, which gives systemverilog); otherwise it is text. Say it explicitly.

docs.title: Flow settings
docs.text:
flow says who does each box of the loop's drawing. A box takes a word, an agent's name, or {by: <word or agent>, ...settings, ...agent options}:

flow:
  generate: claude                              # an agent, no options
  plan: {by: claude, session: pass}             # an agent with options
  validate: flux                                # FluxAgent
  calibrate: off                                # a word

flux is FluxAgent, Flux's own model working a box (its endpoint and model are set in Models and agents). model, its old name, means the same everywhere and is still read; the configurator keeps it in a document that says it and writes flux in a new one. claude, codex and opencode are built in; a server can add agents of its own (named by FLUX_AGENTS). The old form {agent: X} is refused: write {by: X}.

Box Values (first is the default) Purpose flow.validate rules, flux, agent Review the document before the first pass (advisory) flow.orchestrate rules, given, flux, tools, agent, or a search (search settings) What to try next flow.orchestrate.dse adaptive, explore, improve, tune, finetune, variations, or a policy name The emphasis that guides a model or agent (search settings) flow.orchestrate.scope {list: ..., brief: ..., check: ..., timeout_s: 120} The scopes of one whole design a pass may work on (scope) flow.plan off, flux, agent Write the pass's plan, checked before use flow.generate flux, agent, {command: ...}, {catalog: [paths]} Write each design flow.test A command, or an ordered map of named checks; never an agent Decide correctness (checks) flow.measure An ordered map of named stages; never an agent Put numbers on passing designs (measurements) flow.select objectives, agent, {finalists: N} Choose the decision; an agent only breaks ties flow.calibrate on, off Compare a costly stage's numbers with the cheap stage's flow.feedback human, off Take your notes from the loop's Chat into the next prompt flow.knowledge A map (knowledge), or off (an agent may digest and draw lessons) What the model and agents read

The configurator's Graph names the boxes by what they do: orchestrate is Search, generate Design, test Check, measure Measure, select Choose.

  • Words for orchestrate without a search: rules (rules pick the work), given (a fixed order: {given: [part_a, part_b]}), flux (FluxAgent picks), tools (FluxAgent with tools: standings, history, decisions, knowledge), or an agent. Add dse: <emphasis> to guide a model or agent: adaptive (default), explore, improve, tune, finetune, variations, or a policy name (sweep, montecarlo, anneal, gradient, genetic, pareto) as an emphasis. dse guides; it never forbids.
  • orchestrate.scope, for a loop of one whole design (no parts, sub-loops or knobs): each pass works on one scope of it. list is a command printing the scopes, one a line, its name first; brief, given {scope}, prints what the design agent is told of it; check, given {scope} and {artifact}, checks the scope on a design that passed the gate (N failing of M, or its exit). Each pass the orchestrator picks its direction and a scope in one decision, seeing which scopes the latest passes took and how their checks ended (the rules: each in turn). While the scope's check fails, the design goes back to the same agent with the failures, until it is clean or the pass's steps are spent; every design that passes the gate is kept and measured as usual. For a spec kept in the loop's folder: list: fluxpreset ndf list --spec {home}/spec, brief: fluxpreset ndf clauses {scope} --spec {home}/spec (it names the units that depend on it), and fluxpreset ndf scope {scope} --spec {home}/spec lists the unit and its dependents for a check of your own.
  • generate takes exactly one form. {command: ...} is your script (generator contract); {catalog: [a.py, b.py]} reads the listed files (relative to the folder) in turn; flux (FluxAgent) and agents write the design from the brief. A generate agent keeps one session per part through its repairs; session is refused here. A generator command has no timeout_s of its own: it uses the largest check timeout.
  • test and measure are never an agent's. by: on them is refused: they establish facts.
  • select: {finalists: N} is how many designs climb to each costlier stage (default 3). {by: claude, finalists: 2} adds an agent that breaks ties among designs the objectives cannot separate; the objectives' choice stands otherwise.
  • plan is checked before use; a plan that fails the check falls back to the document's order.
  • Thinking. One switch, think: true or false, beside whoever works a box. Where FluxAgent works it -- validate, orchestrate, plan, generate -- {by: flux, think: true} lets it reason before it answers (slower, often better; its thinking shows in the task's live view); think: false, it answers straight. A thinking model's answer that comes back empty is asked again with thinking off. Beside an agent -- any box, critic or Knowledge section an agent works, an agent added under a name of its own too -- {by: claude, think: false} runs it at its effort for not thinking, true at its effort for thinking (both the admin's, below); refused for an agent of your own command. An agent's effort (agent options) is the finer level and wins over its think. Unsaid, the server's thinking by default decides: untouched, FluxAgent answers straight and each agent works at its own effort (no flag), as before. The configurator shows Thinking under the agent wherever one is chosen -- a box, a critic, a Knowledge section -- default, on, off, its help line saying the admin's default, with its effort beside it (FluxAgent's levels or the agent's kind's); a box nothing thinks on shows none. Where FluxAgent works a critic, a Knowledge section or Search under Standard or with tools, the document cannot say its thinking: the two show read-only, the admin's, and the help line says so. FluxAgent proposing the points of a search over settings (Search's AI policy) has its own, written beside it: orchestrate: {by: flux, think: true, effort: high, space: {...}}.
  • Effort (FluxAgent). Beside by: flux (or model) on validate, orchestrate, plan or generate, effort: low | medium | high | max sets FluxAgent's thinking, its tool rounds and its output at once (the table): low 6 rounds, 3000 tokens, no thinking; medium 20 and 6000; high 30 and 10000, thinking; max 50 and 16000, thinking, and a self-check of its answer. It comes before the box's think. Unsaid, the box runs as before (the loop's tool_hops, the run's output cap) unless the admin picked an effort for FluxAgent (thinking by default). The configurator shows effort beside FluxAgent's Thinking.
flow:
  orchestrate: {by: flux, think: true}        # FluxAgent reasons over what to try next
  plan: {by: flux, effort: max}                # thinks, 50 tool rounds, checks its own plan
  generate: {by: codex, think: false}         # the design agent at its effort for not thinking
  select: {by: claude, effort: high}          # the finer level, as it is

docs.title: Critics
docs.text:
A critic is a second opinion on one box, said as critic: inside it. Only four boxes take one:

Box What the critic judges A rejection rounds orchestrate The split into parts, or the pass's direction The work is divided again with the objection yes test A design the checks passed The design fails; the objection is its note on the record no measure A stage's numbers The result is marked rejected and never chosen; it is not measured again no select The pick The decision is made again without it yes 
flow:
  orchestrate: {by: claude, critic: flux}
  test:
    correctness: "{python} {home}/check.py {artifact}"
    critic: claude
  select: {finalists: 2, critic: {by: claude, rounds: 2, timeout_s: 600}}

A critic is flux (FluxAgent), an agent, your own agent ({by: {command: [...]}}), or {by: ..., rounds: N, ...agent options}. rounds (1 to 5, default 1) is how many times the box answers an objection, on orchestrate and select only. A rejection holds for later passes. budget.critique_rounds bounds how often a test critic sends a passing design back; 0 turns the critics off. The older flow.critique is refused; flux task migrate turns it into critics.

docs.title: Check settings
docs.text:
flow.test is one command (a check named test) or an ordered map. Checks run in the order written; the first that reports failures refuses the design and the rest do not run.

test:
  build: "{python} -m py_compile {artifact}"                  # a bare command
  correctness:                                                # or a map
    run: "{python} {home}/check.py {artifact}"
    timeout_s: 60
Field Default Purpose run Required Command string or argument list count_re (\d+) failing One capture group holding the number of failures fail_re Absent One match per failure; used instead of the default count pattern timeout_s 120 Seconds before the check is stopped

Check names are a letter, then letters, digits, _ and -. A check named build uses no default pattern: any non-zero exit means the design did not build. count_re or fail_re at the level of flow.test (not inside a check) is refused. How a check's output becomes a verdict is in the check contract.

docs.title: Measurement settings
docs.text:
flow.measure is an ordered map of stages, cheapest first. A stage is a command or a map:

Field Default Purpose command Required Command string or argument list metrics Required unless metrics_re The names printed as name=value -- a number, or a dictionary (below) metrics_re Derived from metrics Map of metric name to a regex with one capture group needs Inferred for fluxpreset prog count/size; else empty Programs required on PATH; a missing one skips the stage ("NOT RUN") timeout_s 600 Seconds before the stage is stopped cutoff None A gate before the next stage, or a list of gates that must all pass estimate Off Predict first, and skip designs the estimate already rules out

A stage names its metrics only. A metric printed as a dictionary, name={"a": 1, "b": 2} (or inside a JSON object of metrics), is read as one: each finite value becomes name.a, name.b, a test each. Missing, null and non-finite values stay unmeasured, never zero. To rank by the dictionary as a whole, its objective says so: {metric: name, type: dict, aggregate: sum, direction: minimize, unit: us} -- name then holds the aggregate of its tests: mean (default), median, min, max or sum; an objective may instead rank one test, {metric: name.a}. Metric names are unique per stage; evaluator: stages are gone and refused.

Cutoffs gate the next stage: {metric: M, at: N} keeps designs at least N, {metric: M, below: N} at most N, {metric: M, within: F} within the fraction F (0 < F <= 1) of this run's best on that stage. Exactly one rule per condition. M is any number the design has at that stage: measured there or carried from an earlier stage (below).

Estimates: {kind: surrogate|command|model, margin: 0.05}; command only with kind: command (estimate contract). The surrogate needs three measured designs first. A design whose estimate misses a cutoff or a limit by more than the margin is skipped and never measured; designs that run keep their estimate in the record.

Stages measure different things. One stage may time a design and the next measure its area; a stage need not repeat what an earlier one measured. A design's numbers at a stage are, for each metric, the deepest measurement at or before it: a later stage replaces an earlier one's number for the same metric, and a metric only an earlier stage measured is carried forward (the record keeps each stage's own row; the carrying is done when it is read). Results, flux loop results, show and the report say where a carried number came from ("fmax_mhz=500 (from timing)").

flow:
  measure:
    timing: {command: "{python} {home}/sta.py {artifact}", metrics: [fmax_mhz], cutoff: {metric: fmax_mhz, at: 250}}
    area:   {command: "{python} {home}/area.py {artifact}", metrics: [area_um2]}
objectives:
  - {metric: fmax_mhz, goal: ">= 300"}   # judged on area, with timing's number carried
  - {metric: area_um2, direction: minimize}

Every objective must be measured by at least one stage. A limit pinned with stage: must name a stage that has its metric (measured there or before), and a cutoff may name only a metric its stage has; otherwise the run says the question cannot be answered as posed. task check and the run's first step note an objective only the last stage measures: the stages before rank without it.

Between stages: designs that pass a stage's cutoffs join its frontier; the select.finalists best (spread along the frontier with several objectives) climb to the next stage. A stage ranks on the objectives it has numbers for; one not measured yet is left out there, and the log says so ("timing: ranked on fmax_mhz; area_um2 (first on area) not measured yet"). A stage that has no objective at all lets every design through its cutoffs. The decision is made on the deepest stage reached, over the designs measured there, each with every objective by then; a design that never reached the stage where an objective is first measured is not chosen: Results lists it as pending. --screen-only stops after the first stage.

docs.title: Knowledge settings
docs.text:
Field Default Purpose files Empty Files and folders the model reads (specs, sources, notes, PDFs), relative to the folder; a folder is each of its files text Empty Inline context sheet Absent A methods sheet appended to the text digest flux Who summarises the library's papers: flux (FluxAgent) or an agent lessons off Lessons drawn from the record: off, mined, or an agent workbench who digests Who sums up the agents' workbench/ when it changed: off, flux, or an agent ({by: claude, timeout_s: 600} with its options); unsaid, whoever digests the papers ideas off Who cleans up the ideas notebook before a pass, once it grew: off, flux, or an agent; {by: flux, open: 20, new: 10} runs it at 20 open ideas with 10 new since the last cleanup (the defaults). It merges repeated ideas (undoable) and ranks the rest; see Ideas cleanup hidden Empty Files, folders or globs (relative to the folder) the AI agents may not read: tests, checks, a gate's files and their parameters; see Hidden from AI off false off: true turns reading off (lessons, ideas, workbench and hidden may stand beside it); knowledge: off is the same

knowledge: claude is short for {digest: claude}. by: on the knowledge box is refused: say digest:. While knowledge is on, the loop's library/ is read (there is no server-wide library: FLUX_LIBRARY is not read); PDFs go through pdftotext. Each project the loop is linked into has its library inside it, read-only, at library/<project>@<group>/ (<project>@_ for a global project), in the loop's project order, with the project's hidden paths hidden under it: a name with @ at the top of library/ is reserved for them, so the loop's own files and a project's never clash. A project's paper is digested by the loop for its own problem and cited by its place (library/nlu@hw/x.pdf); an exact copy in a later folder is read once.

docs.title: Hidden from AI
docs.text:
knowledge.hidden keeps an agent from gaming the gate by reading it: the loop's own tools (its checks, stages, scripts and probes) read these paths as ever, and a check's failure text still reaches the agent; no agent and no prompt reads them.

flow:
  knowledge:
    hidden: [tests/, golden.py, "params/*.json"]

Each path is relative to the loop folder, inside it, and never the document itself. Sub-loops hide their parent's paths too, beside their own. An agent's own hidden: option adds paths for that agent alone. Hidden paths are left out of the library, the knowledge files, the skills, the workbench's index and flux loop library; flux library, flux loop diff, gate and measure refuse them. Every agent turn's brief names them as off limits, and the agent's own permission settings refuse them:

  • Claude Code: --settings with permissions.deny: Read(...) and Edit(...) on each path (absolute, //..., and relative to the turn's folder when inside it).
  • OpenCode: permission.read and permission.edit deny patterns in its config (OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT).
  • Codex: no per-path rule a user can set; only the brief says so.

No tool is taken away and no shell command is refused for naming a path: the agent keeps its search tools (Claude Code's Grep and Glob, OpenCode's grep and glob) and may run pytest tests. OpenCode's grep and glob follow no read rule, and Claude Code's follow it only best-effort, so there the brief is what asks the agent to leave the paths alone.

This stops an agent from targeting a path; it is no sandbox. A script the agent writes could still open the file, so for secrets use the run's sandbox. In the web app, a file or folder is hidden from the Files tab (Actions, Hide from AI), when it is added, or in the configurator's Knowledge box.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md (front matter name and description, then the instructions). The loop's skills/ folder is read without a word in the document. The model gets an index of them and a skill tool; every coding agent of the loop (the design agent, a box's, a critic, the lessons' and the digests') finds them in its work directory (.claude/skills, .opencode/skills, .agents/skills), together with the built-in flux-loop-commands (how the loop's record is read with flux loop ...).

skills: off                                  # none, not the built-in one either
skills: [skills, ../shared-skills]           # these folders instead of skills/
skills: {off: [flux-loop-commands, rtl-style]}   # skills/ and the built-in one, these two off
skills: {from: [../shared-skills], off: [old-style]}

docs.title: Objective settings
docs.text:
Each entry is a metric name or a map:

Field Default Purpose metric Required A metric a stage reports (name or name.test for a dictionary metric) direction maximize, or the stage metric's minimize or maximize goal None A limit: at most N when minimizing, at least N when maximizing; also ">= 1000", "< 80" stage The deepest stage for a goal Where the goal is judged (a stage that has the metric: measured there or carried from an earlier one) unit Known for common metrics Display unit type number dict: the metric is a dictionary of tests, ranked by aggregate aggregate mean with type: dict How a dictionary's tests make its number: mean, median, min, max, sum tie 0 Relative band within which two designs tie and the next objective decides margin 0 Extra headroom required when a goal is judged on a shallower stage balance false Decide by the best trade-off (the knee) of the goal-less objectives keep None A relative limit: keep this fraction (0..1] of the best gain over above above 0 The reference for keep

How the decision is made: a design that meets every limit beats one that misses any. Among those that meet them, the goal-less objectives decide in the order written (within tie, the next one decides). If none meets every limit, the one missing fewest, then by the smallest shortfall, is reported as the closest, not as a decision. An unmeasured limit counts as missed. With balance, the knee is taken among the designs measured on every balance metric that no other design beats on every objective. An exact tie goes to the next objective in the order written, limits included (of two designs alike on area, the faster), then to the design made first (its first measurement), never to the order the record lists them in: the decision is always on the front. goal cannot be combined with keep or balance; a dictionary metric no objective says type: dict for has no number of its own: an objective names one of its tests (d.test).

docs.title: Run length, repairs, and concurrency
docs.text:
Field Default Purpose passes 0 Passes to run; 0 runs until stopped steps 24 Work items in one pass budget_s None Wall-clock seconds for one pass, checked before each step repair_attempts 12 Repairs of one draft before it is given up batch 1 Search designs one pass carries workers 0 Tool runs at once; 0 = half the cores, at most 4. Use 1 for timings parallel 1 Passes at once (a server limit also applies) parallel_parts 1 Parts drafted at once tools_at_once 0 Checks and measurements at once across the whole loop -- passes and parts at once, and an agent's flux probe -- for a tool that breaks when two of its runs share the machine; 0 = no limit ahead true Measure a part while the next one is drafted screen_only false Stop after the first stage max_depth 3 Deepest nesting of sub-loops regenerate [] Parts to draft again instead of reusing admitted ones exploration_quota 0.0 Least share (0..1) of search choices kept for exploring explore_every 4 Every Nth draft starts fresh rather than from the best explore_after 2 Stalled passes before exploring agent_continues 3 Times a design agent's session is continued past its time limit (the last one is told so). Then the design as it stands is handed in if the gate passes it; else a final short turn (agent_grace_s) whose only job is the gate; else the last file a flux probe gate passed in this design's turns. Only with none of these does the pass give up, without a design, its notes on the record agent_grace_s a quarter of the agent's time limit, 300–600 s The final turn after the continues: told the gate's failure on its file, one gate probe, no stages, no experiments; the last file the gate passed is offered to copy back. Its file is handed in when the gate passes it. 0 turns the final turn off (the passing file, if any, is still handed in) explore 0 Managed by the loop each pass; a value here has no effect cooldown_after 3 Build failures in a row before a part yields patching true Repair with edits rather than full rewrites patch_context_lines 40 Lines around a fault shown in a repair prompt revert_after 3 Failed compile repairs before going back to the last good design regress_after 2 Worsening edits in a row tolerated at first max_tolerance 4 Most that tolerance grows critique_rounds 1 Times a critic may send a passing design back; 0 turns critics off

finalists is set with flow.select.finalists and calibration with flow.calibrate; as budget keys they are refused. Only exploration_quota and prototype values are type-checked; check the others with care.

docs.title: Prototypes
docs.text:
A prototype is the algorithm in Python (or SystemC) checked against the golden model before the target design is written. It applies to problems with a golden model; use false for script-generated designs. Setting it does not create a golden model.

Field Default Purpose prototype true true, false, python, or systemc prototype_attempts 30 First model attempts prototype_patience 8 Attempts earned per new best prototype_attempts_max 90 Most model attempts prototype_agent_attempts 8 First coding-agent attempts prototype_agent_patience 2 Coding-agent attempts earned per new best prototype_agent_attempts_max 20 Most coding-agent attempts prototype_table_max 64 Largest module-level table allowed prototype_cost_max 0 (effective 2000) Cost ceiling before spelling; negative turns it off prototype_shrink_attempts 8 Attempts to make a verified prototype cheaper prototype_unmeasured_stop 4 Unmeasurable attempts in a row before the pass ends

docs.title: Direct-model tools and context
docs.text:
For FluxAgent turns, not a coding agent's.

Field Default Purpose structured true Schema-constrained answers where supported tools true Tools inside model turns compute_timeout_s 10.0 Seconds for the model's compute tool tool_hops 6 Tool rounds before the model must answer hop_share 0.5 Share of the context window for one tool round knowledge_share 0.5 Share of the window for static knowledge compact rules rules or llm: how an over-full context is shortened compact_share 0.6 Window share that triggers compaction tool_result_chars 40000 Most characters of a tool's output given to the model agent [] Model halves turned on: tools, orchestrate, plan (also --agent) plan_file None A saved plan to follow

docs.title: Baseline / pass 0
docs.text:
baseline runs the checks and the real measurements on a reference before pass 1, so results can be read relative to it. It is off by default; pass 0 calls no model or agent, writes no golden model and repairs nothing, and does not count toward passes.

baseline: true                                   # the project as it is: your scripts as written
# baseline: {file: baseline.py}                  # an unchanged design file
# baseline: {command: "{python} {home}/baseline.py {artifact}", timeout_s: 600}
# baseline: {metrics: [{metric: area_um2, value: 120}, {metric: fmax_mhz, value: 1000, stage: place}]}
# add only: true to stop after pass 0
Form What pass 0 measures true Your scripts as written; {artifact} is an empty file, so use {home}/... paths {file: F} F (relative to the folder) copied to {artifact}; the original is untouched {command: C, timeout_s: 600} Whatever C writes to {artifact} (contract); if it writes nothing, the project as it is {metrics: [...]} Nothing runs: the values are recorded as the reference
  • metrics entries are {metric, value, stage}: a finite number; stage defaults to the deepest; the metric must be one that stage reports; each stage/metric pair once. Provided values supply no design and are never the decision.
  • only: true ends the run after pass 0 (a tool check without optimization).
  • Reuse: a successful baseline on record stands while the document's baseline: section is unchanged -- whatever else changes (the folder's files, the tools, Flux). To measure it again, the loop's Settings › Maintenance › Re-Evaluate with Rerun baseline ticked (or flux task run ... --rerun-baseline) makes the next start, and only it, run pass 0. A failed one is tried again at the next start. Baselines bypass the cache, estimates and cutoffs.
  • Baselines are references: drawn as gray lines, the base of relative values, never the decision or a search start. They are not inherited by sub-loops.

docs.title: Parts and sub-loops
docs.text:
parts divides one artifact: parts: [decoder, encoder], a map of descriptions ({decoder: "the 8b10b decoder"}), or decompose (the orchestrator divides it, at most 8). Names are a letter, then letters, digits, _, -. Parts are drafted and checked one by one and joined in order, separated by a blank line.

subtasks divides a problem into child loops: a list of folders beside the document (subtasks: [ops/recip, ops/exp]), inline documents (maps with an id), or decompose. Do not combine parts and subtasks.

  • A folder child has its own problem.yaml (no id; the folder names it), its record is <parent>/<child>, and it shares the parent's out/ and workbench/.
  • Inheritance: a child takes the parent's contract, language, flow (including checks, measurements, space and knowledge), objectives, skills, params, budget and ladder unless it says them; flow, budget and params merge key by key, the child's winning. Not inherited: statement (each child says its own), parts, subtasks, max_subtasks, baseline, and a parent's generate: {command}.
  • Composition: a parent's generate: {command: "... {parts} {artifact}"} composes the children's decided designs into the whole once every child has decided (composition contract). Without it the parent composes nothing.
  • Give inherited skills as paths that resolve from the child too (or absolute ones), and write inline children in the long form ({by: flux}).

docs.title: Improvement ladder
docs.text:
ladder: true turns on the default steps. A map overrides these fields:

Field Default Purpose steps [sweep, take, import, depth, contender, redesign] Improvement actions, in order sweep [2, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32] Pipeline register counts to compare depth_goal 0.8 Target fraction of the incumbent's logic depth redesigns 2 Different algorithms the ladder may ask for per run contender_reach 0.7 Standing at which a contender is considered contender_passes 2 Passes a contender may spend on one incumbent stalls 2 Redesign passes allowed to come back to the same result alone The deepest stage The stage that measures a part on its own

The ladder applies when the problem supports prototypes and parts. Its limits bound those actions; they do not stop an open-ended run. Most loops omit it.
