docs.title: Split a larger design
docs.text: A design too large to write or check in one piece can be split: into parts of one artifact, or into sub-loops, each a loop of its own whose decided designs a parent composes. Use one or the other, never both. The fields are in the Document reference.

docs.title: Parts of one design
docs.text:
parts:
  decoder: the 8b10b decoder
  encoder: the 8b10b encoder

parts is a list of names, a map of names to descriptions, or decompose to let the orchestrator divide the goal itself (into at most 8). Names are a letter, then letters, digits, _ and -. Each part is drafted and checked on its own, then the parts are joined in order, separated by a blank line, and the whole is measured.

Parts suit a model or agent generator that writes one file in pieces. budget.parallel_parts drafts several at once; budget.regenerate (or --regenerate PART) drafts a part again instead of reusing the admitted one.

docs.title: Sub-loops
docs.text:
subtasks: [ops/recip, ops/exp]
flow:
  generate: {command: "{python} {home}/compose.py {parts} {artifact}"}

Each folder in subtasks holds its own problem.yaml, named by its folder (no id). A child inherits the parent's contract, language, flow (checks, measurements, space and knowledge included), objectives, skills, params, budget and ladder unless it says them; flow, budget and params merge key by key, the child's winning. It never inherits statement (each child says its own), parts, subtasks, baseline, or the parent's generate: {command}.

Children share the parent's out/ and workbench/; each child's record is <parent>/<child>. subtasks: decompose lets the orchestrator divide the problem (at most max_subtasks, default 4), and budget.max_depth (default 3) bounds the nesting.

docs.title: Composing the whole
docs.text:
Once every child has decided, the parent's generator command composes their designs into the whole. {parts} is a JSON file mapping each child's name to the path of its decided design:

import json, sys
parts = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))                       # {"recip": "/.../recip.sv", ...}
open(sys.argv[2], "w").write("\n".join(open(p).read() for p in parts.values()))

The whole goes straight to the measurements; it is not checked again, so write and test the composition as carefully as a generator. Without a composition command, the parent composes nothing. A parent that generates with a model or agent can instead draft for its children.

The composition contract has the details, and the NLU example (flux/applications/nlu in the source) shows a larger loop split into child folders.

docs.title: Run, stop, resume
docs.text: Use this page after creating and configuring a loop. In the web app, the same actions are a loop's Start and Stop (Tour). Replace sums with your loop's folder. Commands use the active Flux environment.

docs.title: Check before running
docs.text:
flux task check sums
flux task run sums --passes 1 --json sums/out/answer.json

task check validates the document, lists the stages and required tools, and reports problems before a run: every file the document names must be in the folder (a missing one is listed with the key that names it and what the folder holds), and the golden model must run. It exits 2 when the document does not load (not a task:) and 1 when something is missing or refused (MISSING:, REFUSED:, or WILL NOT RUN: when a flux/fluxpreset command's words are refused by its own --help). Like a run, it runs in the sandbox; --no-sandbox checks on this machine. It is the same check an agent writing the problem runs before it ends its turn. It does not execute the candidate checks and measurements. A bounded first run checks the actual scripts and their output.

A folder normally contains problem.yaml. Additional NAME.problem.yaml files describe alternate problems in the same folder and use separate records. When a folder contains several valid documents, specify the file explicitly for unattended runs:

flux task run sums/small.problem.yaml --passes 1

docs.title: Runtime overrides
docs.text:
Values in budget are persistent settings; command-line options override them for one run. Use flux task run --help for the complete command syntax.

Option Effect --passes N Cap passes; default is budget.passes, or unlimited when omitted/zero --steps N, --repair N Override work per pass and repair attempts per draft --screen-only Stop every design at the first measurement stage --db FILE Use a different record --out FILE Choose where the feasible decision artifact is written --json FILE Write the answer and results as JSON --tui Open the terminal task, log, and results view --model NAME, --think, --num-predict N Choose a model, request reasoning, and bound output tokens --no-structured Disable schema-constrained model output --role ROLE=NAME Override a role; task check lists available choices --agent tools orchestrate plan Give the direct model those tool, orchestration, and planning capabilities; all enables all three --plan FILE Follow a saved loop plan --tool-hops N, --hop-share F, --patience N Override model tool rounds, context share, and prototype patience --regenerate PART... Draft named parts afresh; all starts every part afresh --no-prototype, --no-patching Disable prototype work or edit-based repairs --skill DIR Add a skill directory; repeatable --replies FILE Supply scripted model replies, useful for repeatable experiments --rerun-baseline Measure the baseline (pass 0) again, though the document's baseline is unchanged --reevaluate At this start, after the baseline: check and measure again every design on the record (those Invalidate set aside, else every one), after a check or measurement changed; then the passes --reevaluate-of ID Check and measure again only the designs one invalidation took out (its id is in Results) --remeasure Measure again the designs a rejection asked for, then rest --no-sandbox Run on this machine, not in the sandbox (also FLUX_SANDBOX=0)

docs.title: Stop, resume, and keep experiments separate
docs.text:
An unlimited run continues until you stop it. Limits and timeouts can end individual attempts or passes; a satisfied objective or a stalled search does not automatically end the run. Stop with Ctrl-C, q in the TUI, the browser's Stop action, or another terminal:

flux stop sums/out/sums.db        # finish the current pass
flux stop sums/out/sums.db --now  # interrupt immediately

Run the document again to reuse its record. Cached measurements can be reused; stage commands, the scripts they name, and params contribute to the cache identity. Changing the objective can reuse observations; changing the measurement changes what can be reused.

For a separate experiment, use a fresh --db or a new folder name. Copying a folder's generated out/ and workbench/ also copies its history and agent files; leave them out for a fresh loop. In the browser, a stopped loop's Settings › Preferences › Reset or delete offers Reset, which asks what to keep. Reset removes generated data while retaining the source document and scripts.

For a process that outlives the terminal:

flux run -- flux task run sums
flux status sums/out/sums.db
flux attach sums/out/sums.db

docs.title: Upgrading older loops
docs.text: Flux never upgrades a document silently. flux task migrate FOLDER shows what would change in a loop's documents and --write saves them (the original kept as <file>.orig). A loop's task journal from an earlier version, the file Live reads, is converted once with flux task migrate FOLDER --journal EVENTS (the original kept as events.jsonl.orig.gz); on a server, Admin › Maintenance › Bring task journals up to date does it for every loop.

docs.title: Read the result and full output
docs.text:
flux report sums/out/sums.db
flux log sums/out/sums.db

The report shows measured designs, trade-offs, refusals, and the standing design. The chosen artifact is written under out/ only when a design meets the requirements. An estimated metric or a shallower screening result should not be read as a confirmed measurement.

task run exit Meaning 0 A measured design meets every requirement; the decision artifact is written 3 Correct designs were measured, but none meets every requirement; the report shows the shortfall 1 No design was measured, or the run could not start 130 Interrupted

In the web app, a loop's Live tab shows passes, tools, agent activity, and their output as a tree, a graph, a timeline, and a log. Its Start picker opens an older start; its tasks and conversations belong to that start. Files, logs, and results provide raw or fullscreen views. History is available while its files and records are retained; resetting a loop clears the generated history.

docs.title: Sandbox
docs.text:
flux task check, flux task run and flux ask run inside a container, so neither an agent nor the document's own code (its commands, scripts, golden.py) can touch the rest of the machine. The engine is rootless Podman when installed, else Docker (FLUX_SANDBOX_ENGINE=podman|docker). Without either, these commands stop with the sandbox needs Podman or Docker.

  • It sees the host read-only: the system, /nix/store, Flux itself, the programs on PATH, and the loop's folder (inside, at /sandbox/<loop>/).
  • It writes only the loop's out/ and workbench/, the record's folder, and the loop's own cache under ~/.cache/flux/apps/. Scratch in /tmp is gone after the run.
  • Its home holds the agents' configuration and logins for Flux, not your own home: ~/.ssh, other repositories and the Docker socket are not there.
  • Network is the host's by default. FLUX_SANDBOX_ALLOW=host,domain,10.0.0.0/8 limits HTTP(S) to those destinations; add FLUX_SANDBOX_RAW_NETWORK=1 for direct TCP/UDP to them (needs nft on the host). Behind a proxy, HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY/NO_PROXY pass in (both cases, with localhost added to NO_PROXY); an allowlist's hosts are reached through it. On a server, its admin sets it (Proxy).
  • Limits: FLUX_SANDBOX_MEMORY (e.g. 16g), FLUX_SANDBOX_CPUS, FLUX_SANDBOX_PIDS (default 4096), FLUX_SANDBOX_TMP_SIZE. On a server, its admin's defaults and maximums apply (Sandbox limits).
  • Off: --no-sandbox or FLUX_SANDBOX=0 runs on this machine as you. Use it only for code you trust, such as the first loop.

docs.title: User or system service
docs.text:
scripts/install-service.py (from flux/) writes the units that keep flux serve running and restart it after a commit (flux-update.path).

  • User service (the default): ~/.config/systemd/user/, turned on with systemctl --user daemon-reload && systemctl --user enable --now flux.service flux-update.path. No root needed. It runs only while its user's systemd does: from their login to their last logout, unless root lets it linger (sudo loginctl enable-linger <user>). On Ubuntu, systemd-oomd watches every user@.service and, under memory pressure (50 % for 20 s), kills the user's cgroup that uses the most memory, often the server's with every loop it started; a user unit cannot lower its OOM score, and ManagedOOMPreference=avoid is honoured only on cgroups root owns.
  • System service (--system): run by root's systemd as the owner (User=, Group=; --user NAME), with the same Nix shell, ~/.config/flux/service.env, working folder, KillMode=process, Restart=always, and what only root can set: OOMScoreAdjust=-500 (--oom-score-adjust), ManagedOOMPreference=avoid, OOMPolicy=continue, MemoryLow= with --memory-low 2G. It starts at boot and is outside the user's user@.service. The loop runs it starts are in its cgroup and inherit its OOM score; a sandboxed run's container is Podman's own scope. Rootless Podman keeps its state in /run/user/<uid>: with sandboxed runs, also sudo loginctl enable-linger <user>.

The script runs no sudo: --system writes the units to a folder (a temporary one, or --output DIR; --dry-run prints them) and prints the commands. To switch:

python3 scripts/install-service.py --system -- --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8765
systemctl --user disable --now flux.service flux-update.path      # the user service gives up the port
sudo install -m 0644 -o root -g root /tmp/flux-system-units-*/flux* /etc/systemd/system/
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now flux.service flux-update.path

Back: sudo systemctl disable --now flux.service flux-update.path, remove the three files from /etc/systemd/system/, sudo systemctl daemon-reload, then systemctl --user enable --now flux.service flux-update.path. Never both at once: they would fight over the port.

docs.text:

  • FluxAgent and the coding agents: Models and agents.
  • Following runs in the browser: Web app.

docs.title: First loop
docs.text:
Build a loop that compares two ways to compute the sum of squares of the integers below n. One design loops over the inputs; the other uses a formula. Flux generates both, tests them against a reference, times them, and writes the faster passing design.

This example needs Python 3.11 or newer. It uses no model and no hardware tools.

docs.title: 1. Install Flux
docs.text:
The Flux source is not public: ask its maintainer for access. Then, from its folder (here flux-repo):

cd flux-repo
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -e ./flux
source .venv/bin/activate

If Flux is already installed, use your existing environment. Keep that environment active for the commands below. Hardware tools and the web app are covered in Install.

flux task check and flux task run run inside a container, the sandbox, with rootless Podman (preferred) or Docker. Without either, they stop with the sandbox needs Podman or Docker. This example runs only your own scripts, so you can run it on your machine directly:

export FLUX_SANDBOX=0        # or add --no-sandbox to each flux task command

docs.title: 2. Create the folder and document
docs.text:
flux new sums

Replace sums/problem.yaml with:

statement: Find the fastest correct sum_squares(n) implementation.
contract: >-
  Provide sum_squares(n) for nonnegative integers n. Return the exact integer
  sum of i*i for 0 <= i < n. Keep the function name and signature.
language: python

flow:
  orchestrate:
    policy: sweep
    space:
      implementation: [loop, formula]
  generate:
    command: ["{python}", "{home}/render.py", "{artifact}", "{implementation}"]
  test:
    correctness: "{python} {home}/check.py {artifact}"
  measure:
    bench:
      command: "{python} {home}/bench.py {artifact}"
      metrics: [time_ms]

objectives:
  - {metric: time_ms, direction: minimize}

budget: {passes: 2, steps: 1, workers: 1, prototype: false}

The folder name sums identifies the loop and its record; you do not add an id field. space has two choices, so this first run has two passes, one design per pass. workers: 1 keeps the timed measurements from competing with each other.

docs.title: 3. Write the generator
docs.text:
Create sums/render.py:

import sys
from pathlib import Path

implementations = {
    "loop": "sum(i * i for i in range(n))",
    "formula": "n * (n - 1) * (2 * n - 1) // 6",
}
expression = implementations[sys.argv[2]]
Path(sys.argv[1]).write_text(f"def sum_squares(n):\n    return {expression}\n")

Flux replaces {implementation} with the selected knob value and {artifact} with the path where this script must write the design. {home} is the loop folder; {python} is the interpreter running Flux. See command placeholders.

docs.title: 4. Write the correctness check
docs.text:
Create sums/check.py:

import importlib.util
import sys

try:
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("candidate", sys.argv[1])
    candidate = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    spec.loader.exec_module(candidate)
    function = candidate.sum_squares
except Exception as exc:
    print(f"did not load: {exc}")
    sys.exit(3)

failures = 0
for n in [0, 1, 2, 10, 100, 1000]:
    expected = sum(i * i for i in range(n))
    try:
        actual = function(n)
    except Exception as exc:
        actual = repr(exc)
    if actual != expected:
        failures += 1
        print(f"FAIL n={n}: got {actual!r}, expected {expected}")
print(f"{failures} failing")
sys.exit(1 if failures else 0)

This is the gate, the loop's checks: a failing design never reaches the benchmark. Exit 3 means the design could not build or load; exit 1 means it loaded but failed the tests. These six cases are this example's test coverage, not a proof for every possible input.

docs.title: 5. Write the measurement
docs.text:
Create sums/bench.py:

import importlib.util
import sys
import time

spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("candidate", sys.argv[1])
candidate = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
spec.loader.exec_module(candidate)
candidate.sum_squares(1_000_000)  # warm up

times = []
for _ in range(9):
    started = time.perf_counter()
    candidate.sum_squares(1_000_000)
    times.append((time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000)
print(f"time_ms={min(times):.6f}")

metrics: [time_ms] tells Flux which name=value output to read. The objective asks it to minimize that number. The benchmark workload, repetition count, and statistic are your choice; here they make the difference between a loop and a formula easy to see.

docs.title: 6. Check, run, and inspect
docs.text:
flux task check sums
flux task run sums --json sums/out/answer.json
flux report sums/out/sums.db

task check validates the document and lists its requirements; it does not run the candidate tests or benchmark. The run executes them and stops after the two passes in budget. The formula should win this workload; the actual times come from your machine.

The run writes, among other bookkeeping files:

File Contents sums/out/sums.py The chosen passing design sums/out/sums.db The record: every design, check and measurement sums/out/answer.json The decision and recorded results sums/out/sums-report.html The report generated by flux report

Keep the record to reuse previous measurements. To try a separate experiment, copy the loop folder to a new name and omit its generated out/ and workbench/ directories.

docs.title: Change the loop
docs.text:
Add another implementation to render.py and space.implementation, then raise budget.passes or override it with --passes 3. You can replace the generator with an agent, change the benchmark, add a second measurement stage, or introduce a limit alongside the speed objective.

Continue with Configure, then Search and agents, or open the loop in the web app. For another starting point, copy a folder from flux/applications/, including its scripts, or use flux new NAME for a blank loop.

docs.title: Agent options
docs.text: The options a coding agent takes in a document. Which boxes an agent may work is in the Document reference; where its model and login come from is in Models and agents.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Beside by: <agent> on any box an agent may work, or on a critic:

docs.title: What an agent may run
docs.text: An agent never compiles, simulates or tests by itself: those programs are denied (verilator, yosys, openroad, sta, klayout, champsim, gcc, g++, cc, c++, clang, clang++, make, cmake, ninja, pytest, bash, sh, flux rtl, flux task, flux run) unless allow gives them back. It checks its file through the loop's own gate and stages with flux probe; probe: false keeps it from running any of them itself (the loop alone checks and measures), and budget.tools_at_once makes its probes wait for a free slot like the loop's own runs. The agent's model is set on the machine (FLUX_<NAME>_MODEL or the web's Agents settings), not in the document. Your own agent is by: {command: [my-agent, "{prompt_file}", "{artifact}"]} (agent contract).

    probe               Inside an agent's turn: check a file with the loop's
                        own gate or stage.
    loop                What a loop already knows, read back: its summary,
                        passes, ideas, designs tried, results, designs
                        compared, events, a design, papers; its gate on a
                        file.
    knowledge           The accepted knowledge of the projects a loop reads:
                        list, search, show.
    library             A loop's library read in pieces: list, search, digest,
                        outline, read.
    serve               The web interface: accounts, loops, runs followed
                        live.
    user                The web interface's accounts, from the server's
                        machine.
    project             The web interface's projects (a group's, or global),
                        from the server's machine.
    web-loop            The web interface's loops, from the server's machine:
                        list, start, stop, status.
    web-agent           The web interface's users' agents, from the server's
                        machine: their gate, their Test.
    selftest            Check this machine: a command-driven loop, the model,
                        optional application tools.
    new                 Write a loop's baseline to fill in: the skeleton
                        problem.yaml, a README of the folder's parts,
                        library/.
    consult             A question about a loop, answered by an agent that
                        reads it and changes nothing.
    chat                A message in the web's Chat, answered by an agent

    login               A coding agent's login, its home a given folder (an

usage: flux loop [-h]
                 {summary,passes,notes,show,ideas,tried,results,compare,events,design,diff,library,digest,gate,measure} ...

Reads a loop's record and library. Inside an agent's turn it reads that turn's
loop; elsewhere --loop (a folder, a document or a record file; default: the
current folder). Reads add nothing to the record and open it read-only, so a
record in use is safe.

  {summary,passes,notes,show,ideas,tried,results,compare,events,design,diff,library,digest,gate,measure}
    summary             The loop in short: the baseline, the best per
                        objective and the standing pick, each against the
                        baseline at the same stage.
    passes              Each pass, oldest first: its search direction and why,
                        what it decided.
    notes               The operator's notes and the decisions' reasons,
                        oldest first.
    show                One design: its idea and why, every stage's numbers or
                        error, its trace files.
    ideas               The ideas notebook: each hypothesis, its status and
                        the evidence on record.
    tried               The designs tried, oldest first: the stages each
                        reached, its numbers or why it stopped.
    results             The measured designs at one stage, ranked by the
                        loop's objectives, with every metric each has (a
                        dictionary metric's cases as metric.case).
    compare             Designs side by side, metric by metric, the best on
                        each objective marked; how far each got and why it
                        stopped.
    events              The record's events: without --kind how many of each
                        kind; with it the last N of that kind (decision,
                        conclusion, pass, human_note, idea, decided:...), each
                        in short.

                        start of one).

                        library`, as it answered).

                        of `flux library digest`).

docs.title: Commands and placeholders
docs.text: Every command a document names runs the same way, receives the same placeholders, and follows a contract: its arguments, what it prints, its exit code.

docs.title: How commands run
docs.text:
Every command a document names (checks, stages, estimates, the generator, the search, the baseline, the composition) runs the same way. Your own agent's command differs; see agent command.

  • Written as a list of arguments or one string. A string is split like a shell would split it, but no shell runs: for a pipe or redirection, call one yourself: ["sh", "-c", "cat {artifact} | wc -l"].
  • flux first runs Flux's own CLI with the same interpreter (flux tools ...).
  • fluxpreset first runs one of Flux's presets the same way (fluxpreset rtl measure ...).
  • Working directory is {workdir}, the pass's trace folder, shared by every design in the pass. Name your files with {home}/...; relative paths do not reach the loop's folder.
  • Environment: Flux's own, unchanged. Nothing is added.
  • Standard input: inherited from Flux, not data. A command must not read stdin.
  • Output: stdout and stderr are captured separately; checks and stages read both, joined. Line endings are normalised. Live shows the command, its folder, the ends of its output as it runs, and its exit.
  • Timeouts stop the whole process group. A missing program is reported as "not found on PATH" before the run; flux task check lists them.
  • Placeholders are replaced inside every argument, without quoting. At load, a {name} that is neither the loop's nor a knob is refused (an argument containing spaces, such as an sh -c script, is not checked). A placeholder with no value for that command is passed through as written.

docs.title: Command placeholders
docs.text:
Placeholder Value Generator Check, stage, estimate Search Baseline Composition {artifact} Path of the design file (<workdir>/<name><ext>) writes it reads it "" writes it writes the whole {home} The document's folder (absolute) ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ {workdir} The pass's working folder ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ the compose folder {python} The interpreter running Flux ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ {name} The design's name (mul8#3, slice_sieve) ✓ ✓ search ✓ the loop's id {part} The part being drafted, else "" ✓ "" "" "" "" {params} Path of a JSON file of params ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ {knob} One knob's value (True/False for booleans) search mode ✓ first choices {point} Path of a JSON file of every knob search mode ✓ "" ✓ "" {failure} Why the last attempt was refused (text) drafting "" {attempt} 1, 2, ... drafting 1 {history}, {state} Search history and the search's own state file ✓ {parts} Path of a JSON map of the children's designs ✓ {scope} The scope a pass works on, in orchestrate.scope's brief and check {prompt}, {prompt_file}, {session}, {answer} Brief and session, for your own agent

File formats:

  • {params} is params.json in {workdir}: the document's params as a JSON object (a sub-loop's merged over its parent's), rewritten for every command.
  • {point} is <artifact>.point.json: the knobs as a JSON object, components nested ({"algorithm": "list_sieve", "prefetch": {"distance": 2}}); an optional component that is off is left out.
  • {failure} is the text itself, not a file: the last 4000 characters of the failing check's output (prefixed failed at <check>: with several checks), or a send-back reason. It is empty on the first attempt.
  • {parts} is parts.json in the compose folder: {"<child name>": "<absolute path of its decided design>"}, in declared order.

docs.title: Generator command
docs.text:
generate: {command: ...} writes one design to {artifact}. Its stdout is not the design.

Drafting (no space): each draft is checked; if the checks refuse it, the command runs again with {failure} and {attempt} set, up to budget.repair_attempts times. A failing command (non-zero exit, or exit 0 without the file) ends the repairs at once; so does writing the same design twice.

Search (with a space): the command runs once per proposed point, with that point's {knob}s and {point}. A failing command drops the point; there is no repair. The design is named after its knob values.

# document: generate: {command: "{python} {home}/gen.py {artifact} {attempt} {failure}"}
import sys
out, attempt, failure = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]), sys.argv[3]   # failure is "" at first
design = "def count_primes(n):\n    ...\n" if not failure else "...a design that fixes it..."
open(out, "w").write(design)                                         # exit 0

docs.title: Check command
docs.text:
A check reads {artifact} and reports failures. Flux reads stdout and stderr together:

  1. Exit 3 means the design did not build, whatever was printed. For a check named build, any non-zero exit means that.
  2. Otherwise, with count_re (default (\d+) failing): the first match's number is the failure count. With fail_re only: each match is one failure.
  3. With no match: exit 0 passes, any other exit is one failure.

A printed count wins over the exit code: 2 failing with exit 0 fails, and 0 failing with exit 1 passes. The first check with failures refuses the design; its output (last 4000 characters) is what Live shows and what a model or agent gets back to repair. A check's debug output on stderr never fails it unless a pattern matches there.

# document: test: {correctness: "{python} {home}/check.py {artifact}"}
import importlib.util, sys
try:
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("design", sys.argv[1])
    design = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(design)
except Exception as exc:
    print(f"did not load: {exc}"); sys.exit(3)                 # 3: did not build
cases = {10: 4, 100: 25, 1000: 168}
bad = [n for n, want in cases.items() if design.count_primes(n) != want]
for n in bad:
    print(f"FAIL n={n}: got {design.count_primes(n)}, expected {cases[n]}")
print(f"{len(bad)} failing of {len(cases)}")
sys.exit(1 if bad else 0)

docs.title: Measurement command
docs.text:
A stage reads {artifact} and prints its numbers. It must exit 0; on any other exit its numbers are discarded and the design is refused at that stage. Flux reads stdout and stderr:

  • name=value, at the start of a line or after a space: the first occurrence of each metric counts. value is a number (1.5, -2e3); nan and inf are unmeasured.
  • A JSON object on a line of its own (it may span lines): its keys that are declared metrics are read. A name=value line overrides it.
  • A dictionary metric is name={"test": 12, "other": null} (the last occurrence counts).
  • metrics_re, if given, replaces the name=value patterns: one capture group each.

Exit 0 with no metric found refuses the design ("no metric matched in the output"). A stage that reports only some of its metrics is still recorded with those it did. For timings, set budget.workers: 1: runs at the same time disturb each other.

# document: measure: {bench: {command: "{python} {home}/bench.py {artifact}", metrics: [time_ms]}}
import importlib.util, statistics, sys, time
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("design", sys.argv[1])
design = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(design)
runs = []
for _ in range(5):
    t = time.perf_counter(); design.count_primes(1_000_000); runs.append((time.perf_counter() - t) * 1e3)
print(f"time_ms={statistics.median(runs):.3f} time_spread_ms={max(runs) - min(runs):.3f}")

The measurement cache: a design measured once by a stage is not measured again while nothing that stage depends on changes: the design's text (or knobs), the stage's command, metrics and patterns, params, the knobs the command names, the files in the folder (except out/, runs/, workbench/, library/ and the documents), the {home}/... files the command names, and the builds of its programs and needs. Change any of them and it is measured again. Only successful measurements are cached.

docs.title: Estimate command
docs.text:
estimate: {kind: command, command: ..., margin: 0.1} runs before the stage, once for each design the cache does not hold, with the stage's placeholders and timeout. It prints the stage's metrics in the same format. A non-zero exit or no numbers means no estimate: the tool runs. A design whose estimate misses a cutoff or a limit by more than margin (a fraction of the limit) is skipped and recorded as refused by the estimate.

# document: estimate: {kind: command, command: "{python} {home}/estimate.py {artifact}"}
import sys
print(f"time_ms={len(open(sys.argv[1]).read()) * 0.01:.3f}")

docs.title: Search command
docs.text:
orchestrate: {command: ..., timeout_s: 600} is your own search. Each round, Flux writes {history} and runs the command; the command answers with JSON on stdout.

{history} (search-history.json in {workdir}):

{"measured": [{"name": "w4", "knobs": {"w": 4}, "stage": "bench", "metrics": {"time_ms": 3.1}, "by": "mine"}],
 "refused":  [{"name": "w9", "why": "failed at correctness: 2 failing"}],
 "guidance": "operator notes, if any",
 "round": 3}

{state} (out/<record>.search-state.json) is yours: read it if it exists, write it every round; it survives restarts.

The answer is the last line of stdout that is a JSON object (or the whole stdout):

Key Meaning candidates [{name, artifact, knobs, why, by}]: name required; artifact is the design's text (not a path); knobs reach the checks and stages as {knob}/{point} lessons Lines added to the run's lessons not_established Lines added to the report conclusion What the search concluded, recorded when nothing is decided say A line printed with the round done true: this is the last batch

No candidates also ends the search. Candidates go straight to the checks and stages; the generator does not run for them. A non-zero exit or no JSON ends the search with a note.

# document: orchestrate: {command: "{python} {home}/search.py {history} {state}", timeout_s: 300}
import json, os, sys
history, state_path = json.load(open(sys.argv[1])), sys.argv[2]
state = json.load(open(state_path)) if os.path.exists(state_path) else {"next": 1}
tried = {m["name"] for m in history["measured"]} | {r["name"] for r in history["refused"]}
cands = [{"name": f"w{w}", "artifact": f"WIDTH = {w}\n", "knobs": {"w": w}, "why": "next width"}
         for w in (state["next"], state["next"] + 1) if f"w{w}" not in tried]
state["next"] += 2
os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(state_path), exist_ok=True)
json.dump(state, open(state_path, "w"))
print(json.dumps({"candidates": cands, "done": state["next"] > 8}))

docs.title: Baseline command
docs.text: baseline: {command: ...} runs once, before pass 1, with the first point (every knob's first choice, overlaid with the first seed). It either writes the reference design to {artifact}, or prepares the project and writes nothing (then the checks and stages run on the project, through {home}/... paths). A non-zero exit records "baseline failed" and the loop goes on.

docs.title: Composition command
docs.text:
A parent with subtasks and generate: {command: "{python} {home}/compose.py {parts} {artifact}"} runs it once every child has decided. {parts} maps each child to its decided design's path; the command writes the whole to {artifact}. The whole goes to the measurements directly (it is not checked again). A failure leaves no whole, with a note in the report.

import json, sys
parts = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))                       # {"recip": "/.../recip.sv", ...}
open(sys.argv[2], "w").write("\n".join(open(p).read() for p in parts.values()))

docs.title: Agent command
docs.text:
Your own coding agent: by: {command: [my-agent, "--prompt", "{prompt_file}"], output: text, resume: [...]}. Write command as a list.

  • Placeholders use Python formatting: {prompt} (the brief; very long briefs become an instruction to read the file), {prompt_file}, {artifact}, {workdir} (the session folder), {part}, {name}, {python}, {home}, {workbench}, {probe}; a resume command also gets {session} and {answer}. Write a literal brace as {{ or }}; an unknown name refuses the draft.
  • The brief goes to stdin unless the command names {prompt}, {prompt_file} or {answer}.
  • It runs in its session folder with Flux's environment, plus FLUX_<NAME>_ENV and FLUX_PROBE. Default timeout 1800 s.
  • It writes {artifact}. If it does not, its reply is read: a JSON artifact field, else the largest fenced code block.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
The words Flux and its web app use, one term each.

Loop. A folder holding a document, problem.yaml, and the scripts and files it names. The folder's name is the loop's id. Flux generates designs, checks and measures them, and decides, pass after pass.

Document. The loop's problem.yaml: what to make (statement, contract), who does each box (flow), what wins (objectives) and how much to spend (budget). See the Document reference.

Start. One launch of a loop, from Start (or flux task run) until it stops. A loop keeps one log and one record across its starts; each start resumes from the record.

Pass. One trip round the loop: choose what to try, make a design, check it, measure it, decide. budget.passes or --passes N caps them; without a cap a run goes on until stopped.

Box. One step of the loop as the configurator's Graph draws it, ten in all. Setup, before the passes: Validate (validate), Plan (plan), Knowledge (knowledge) and Notes (feedback). Each pass: Search (orchestrate), Design (generate), Check (test), Measure (measure, its calibration too) and Choose (select). Then Record, always on. flow says who works each box.

Check. A command that decides whether a design is correct (flow.test). Checks run in the order written; the first that reports failures refuses the design. Together they are the gate: a design that fails it is never measured.

Measurement. A command that puts numbers on a design that passed the gate. Each measurement is a stage of flow.measure; stages run cheapest first, and a cutoff decides which designs go on to the next.

Design. One candidate the loop made: a file (the artifact) written by a script, a model or an agent, with its checks and measurements on the record.

Design name. Each pass's design takes the next number, a new draft or an edit of the standing design alike: pass 1 primes#1, pass 2 primes#2 (from primes#1), pass 3 primes#3 (from primes#1). The numbers go on after a stop and a restart. Inside a pass, the tries are primes#3, primes#3.2, primes#3.3 ...; the try the gate passes is the pass's design and is named primes#3. A refused try goes on the record under its own text (primes#3~1a2b3c). A pass none of whose tries passed spends its number, so the record can have gaps. Two designs whose texts differ only in spacing, or in comments (Python, Verilog, SystemVerilog, C, C++), are the same design: a draft that repeats a measured one is refused before it is built ("the same as primes#1"). A search's points (arch=ripple) and a composition of parts keep names of their own.

Standing design. The design the next pass builds on: the last decision on the record (with nothing that meets every limit, the closest). A run started again keeps it.

Decision. The design that meets every limit and is best on the objectives. Flux writes it under out/. When none meets every limit, the closest is reported, not decided. "Then earliest" after its Decided by means another accepted design ties it on every objective: the one made first (measured first) is the decision.

Record. The SQLite file a loop writes, out/<id>.db: every design, check, measurement and refusal, with where it came from. A rerun reuses it.

Campaign. The command line's word for one line of work inside a record, named after the loop. --campaign on flux report, flux stop and the others picks one; by default, the latest.

Objective, limit, preference. An objective is a metric and a direction. With a goal it is a limit (at least or at most a value); without one it is a preference, compared in the order written.

Front, knee. The front (Pareto frontier) is the set of designs no other design beats on every objective at once. The knee is where improving one objective starts to cost much more of another.

Knob, space. A knob is one setting with a list of choices; the space is all of them (flow.orchestrate.space). A point is one choice for every knob.

Search policy. How the next points are chosen: sweep, montecarlo, gradient, anneal, genetic, pareto, flux (FluxAgent), and others. See Search policies.

Part, sub-loop. A part is a piece of one design, written and checked on its own (parts). A sub-loop is a child loop in its own folder (subtasks), whose decided designs a parent can compose. See Split a larger design.

FluxAgent. Flux's own language model, on an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, as a worker: flux in a document (generate: flux, {by: flux}), a chat or --author; model, its old name, is the same. It can propose points, write designs, review the document, digest papers and answer in Chat.

Agent. A coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or one a server adds) that takes a brief and writes files. It runs on its own model settings, never on Flux's. See Models and agents.

Critic. A second opinion on a box: Search (the split), Check (each design its checks passed), Measure (a stage's numbers) or Choose (the pick), each set in its box's panel in the configurator's Graph. Its rejection is a verdict: the work is divided again, the design fails, the numbers are marked, or the pick is made again. See critics.

Author. In flux ask and New loop › Agent, FluxAgent or an agent that writes the document and its files from your prompt.

Knowledge, library. What the model and agents read besides the document: the files and text in flow.knowledge, the loop's library/ of papers, and lessons from the record.

Ideas notebook. The hypotheses the loop's model and agents proposed, each with the designs that tested it, kept across passes (Results › Ideas). The ideas cleanup merges repeated ideas into one; a merged idea is kept, folded under the one it was merged into. Each idea has a number, said "idea 3" (oldest first), so it is never taken for design #3.

Skill. A folder with a SKILL.md (a name, a description, then instructions) that the model and agents can load. The loop's skills/ folder is read by default.

Workbench. The agents' own folder beside the document, workbench/: tools they build and notes they keep, shared by the loop's agents and kept across runs.

Chat. A conversation with an agent or FluxAgent that belongs to no loop, in the web app's Chat tab. It may read your loops (read-only) and keep tools and notes in your chat workbench, one folder for all your chats, as the admin allows and you switch on. See Chat.

Hidden from AI. Paths no agent or prompt may read, such as the gate's tests (knowledge.hidden). The loop's own commands still read them.

Golden model. A short Python file, usually golden.py, that says what a hardware design must compute (PORTS and golden(**inputs)), not how. See Presets.

Prototype. The algorithm written first in Python (or SystemC) and checked against the golden model before the hardware design is written.

Baseline. A reference measured before pass 1 (pass 0), such as the design you have today. Results can be read relative to it; it is never the decision.

Preset. One of Flux's own checks and measurements, run as fluxpreset NAME. See Presets.

Archived loop. A stopped loop kept read-only: its record, document, files, workbench, last log, Chat and task journals stay; its pass folders, tool outputs, caches, scratch and older logs are deleted. The loop lists show it under Archived; Unarchive makes it editable again. See Archive.

Sandbox. The container flux task check, flux task run and flux ask run in, so a loop's code and agents cannot touch the rest of the machine. See Run, stop, resume.

ULP. A unit in the last place: the gap between two neighbouring floating-point numbers. "Within 1 ULP" means at most one step from the exact result.

ASAP7. A free, predictive 7 nm process design kit from Arizona State University. Flux's area, timing and power numbers are on ASAP7, not on a commercial process.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text:
Flux's own checks and measurements. A document runs one as fluxpreset NAME ...; nothing is copied into the loop's folder. flux tools lists the catalog entries below, and the configurator offers them as a check's Type or a measurement's Tool under Flux presets. In a shell, fluxpreset alone lists the presets and fluxpreset NAME --help describes one.

Each entry gives its title, catalog id and role, the command a document writes, and its parameters with their defaults. A {name} in a command that is not one of the loop's placeholders is a parameter.

docs.title: golden
docs.text:
The golden test for RTL: the design against a golden model's vectors. It prints the failing vectors and N failing of M, and exits 0 (pass), 1 (fail) or 3 (did not compile). --extra F.sv adds a module the design instantiates. The golden model's format is below.

fluxpreset golden DESIGN --golden golden.py [--extra F.sv] [--module M]
  • Test against a golden model (rtl-golden, a check): fluxpreset golden {artifact} --golden {golden} Verilator runs the module on golden.py's vectors and counts the wrong outputs. Parameters: golden ({home}/golden.py). Reports N failing. Needs verilator.

docs.title: rtl
docs.text:
Hardware checks and measurements on the ASAP7 process: lint with Verilator, measure with OpenROAD-flow-scripts. rtl measure runs the flow to the stage asked and prints one line, fmax_mhz=... area_um2=... power_w=... cell_count=... path_ps=... worst_slack_ps=... (stat only area and cells; route adds drc_errors and wirelength_um).

fluxpreset rtl lint DESIGN
fluxpreset rtl measure DESIGN --stage stat|synth|place|route --clock-ps N
fluxpreset rtl cycles DESIGN --golden golden.py
fluxpreset rtl equiv DESIGN --reference ref.sv
fluxpreset rtl breakdown DESIGN
fluxpreset rtl fmax DESIGN --stage synth [--steps 6]
fluxpreset rtl power DESIGN --golden golden.py --stage place
fluxpreset rtl energy DESIGN --golden golden.py --stage place
fluxpreset rtl path DESIGN --stage place
  • Lint for hardware defects (rtl-lint, a check): fluxpreset rtl lint {artifact} Verilator's hardware defects only: latches, multiple drivers, combinational loops, blocking/non-blocking mixes, implicit nets; width and style warnings are not defects. It also refuses what does not parse. Reports N failing. Needs verilator.
  • Area and cells (ASAP7) (rtl-stat, a stage): fluxpreset rtl measure {artifact} --stage stat --clock-ps {clock_ps} OpenROAD-flow-scripts' synthesis: the mapped cells' area; nothing timed, the cheapest screen. Parameters: clock_ps (1000). Reports area_um2, cell_count. Needs yosys, openroad, make.
  • Synthesise and time (ASAP7) (rtl-synth, a stage): fluxpreset rtl measure {artifact} --stage synth --clock-ps {clock_ps} OpenROAD-flow-scripts to its floorplan: the netlist timed unplaced, seconds. Parameters: clock_ps (1000). Reports fmax_mhz, area_um2, power_w, cell_count, path_ps. Needs yosys, openroad, make, sta.
  • Place and time (ASAP7) (rtl-place, a stage): fluxpreset rtl measure {artifact} --stage place --clock-ps {clock_ps} OpenROAD-flow-scripts to detailed placement, timed with wire estimates: tens of seconds. Parameters: clock_ps (1000). Reports fmax_mhz, area_um2, power_w, cell_count, path_ps. Needs yosys, openroad, make, sta.
  • Route and time (ASAP7) (rtl-route, a stage): fluxpreset rtl measure {artifact} --stage route --clock-ps {clock_ps} OpenROAD-flow-scripts to routing: timing after global routing, minutes. Parameters: clock_ps (1000). Reports fmax_mhz, area_um2, power_w, cell_count, path_ps. Needs yosys, openroad, make, sta.
  • Clock cycles (Verilator) (rtl-cycles, a stage): fluxpreset rtl cycles {artifact} --golden {golden} A clocked design run on golden.py's vectors, each started when the last is done: its latency in cycles (the most, the fewest) and the mean cycles per result. Parameters: golden ({home}/golden.py). Reports latency_cycles, latency_min_cycles, cycles_per_result. Needs verilator.
  • Equal to a reference module (rtl-equiv, a check): fluxpreset rtl equiv {artifact} --reference {reference} Formal equivalence with Yosys (a miter of the two, proved by SAT; a clocked pair by induction): passes when they are equal for every input, else prints a counterexample. Parameters: reference ({home}/reference.sv). Reports N failing. Needs yosys.
  • Where the area goes (ASAP7) (rtl-breakdown, a stage): fluxpreset rtl breakdown {artifact} --clock-ps {clock_ps} OpenROAD-flow-scripts' synthesis, its cells grouped: sequential, adders, XORs, buffers and inverters, the rest of the logic; and the flops. Parameters: clock_ps (1000). Reports area_seq_um2, area_arith_um2, area_xor_um2, area_buf_um2, area_logic_um2, flop_count, area_um2. Needs yosys, openroad, make.
  • Fastest clock that closes (ASAP7) (rtl-fmax, a stage): fluxpreset rtl fmax {artifact} --stage {stage} --clock-ps {clock_ps} --steps {steps} A few OpenROAD-flow-scripts runs, each at the period the last one's slack says, until the fastest clock that closes timing at that stage is found: costly, and the honest fmax. Parameters: stage (synth), clock_ps (1000), steps (6). Reports fmax_closed_mhz, closed_period_ps. Needs yosys, openroad, sta, make.
  • Power from the design's own switching (ASAP7) (rtl-power, a stage): fluxpreset rtl power {artifact} --golden {golden} --stage {stage} --clock-ps {clock_ps} Verilator runs golden.py's vectors and records the switching; OpenROAD reads it on the synthesised or placed design and reports power: internal, switching, leakage. Parameters: golden ({home}/golden.py), stage (place), clock_ps (1000). Reports power_w, power_internal_w, power_switching_w, power_leakage_w. Needs verilator, yosys, openroad, sta, make.
  • Energy per result (ASAP7) (rtl-energy, a stage): fluxpreset rtl energy {artifact} --golden {golden} --stage {stage} --clock-ps {clock_ps} The power the golden vectors' own switching draws, times the time one result takes (its measured cycles at the clock): energy per result and energy-delay product. Parameters: golden ({home}/golden.py), stage (place), clock_ps (1000). Reports energy_pj_per_result, edp_pj_ns, power_w, cycles_per_result. Needs verilator, yosys, openroad, sta, make.
  • The critical path's anatomy (ASAP7) (rtl-path, a stage): fluxpreset rtl path {artifact} --stage {stage} --clock-ps {clock_ps} OpenROAD's worst path at the stage: how many cells it crosses, and how much of its delay is in the cells and how much in the wires -- whether to cut logic or wire. Parameters: stage (place), clock_ps (1000). Reports path_ps, path_levels, path_cell_ps, path_wire_ps, slack_ps. Needs yosys, openroad, sta, make.

docs.title: systemc
docs.text:
A SystemC design as SystemVerilog: ICSC translates it, so every RTL preset can judge it. Alone it checks that the module translates; --then "golden --golden g.py" or --then "rtl measure --stage stat" runs that preset on the translation.

fluxpreset systemc DESIGN.h --top M --golden golden.py [--then "golden --golden golden.py"]
  • SystemC translates to RTL (ICSC) (systemc-translate, a check): fluxpreset systemc {artifact} --top {top} --golden {golden} ICSC translates the SystemC module to SystemVerilog: passes when it does, and when the ports are the golden model's. Parameters: top (top), golden ({home}/golden.py). Reports N failing.
  • SystemC against a golden model (systemc-golden, a check): fluxpreset systemc {artifact} --top {top} --golden {golden} --then "golden --golden {golden}" ICSC translates the SystemC module, then Verilator runs the RTL on golden.py's vectors. Parameters: top (top), golden ({home}/golden.py). Reports N failing. Needs verilator.

docs.title: cases
docs.text:
The golden test for Python: the design's function called on cases and compared with the expected value or a reference function's (floats within --tol). Cases come from a JSON table ([args] or {"args", "kwargs", "expected"}), the reference module's CASES, and --random N draws of its inputs(rng).

fluxpreset cases DESIGN.py --call F [--reference ref.py[:F]] [--cases cases.json] [--random N] [--tol R]
  • Compare with a reference function (python-cases, a check): fluxpreset cases {artifact} --call {call} --reference {reference} --random {random} Calls the design's function on cases (a JSON table, the reference's CASES, random inputs from its inputs(rng)) and compares each result with the reference function's or the expected value. Parameters: call (main), reference ({home}/reference.py), random (100). Reports N failing.

docs.title: ccases
docs.text:
cases for a C or C++ function: the design built as a shared library and called through ctypes with a scalar --sig, against a Python reference.

fluxpreset ccases DESIGN.c --call F --sig "long(long,long)" --reference ref.py:F --random N
  • Compare a C function with a reference (c-cases, a check): fluxpreset ccases {artifact} --call {call} --sig {sig} --reference {reference} --random {random} Builds the design as a shared library and calls one function (a scalar signature) on cases, each result compared with a Python reference function's or the expected value. Parameters: call (main), sig (int(int)), reference ({home}/reference.py), random (100). Reports N failing. Needs cc.

docs.title: pytest
docs.text:
Your pytest file against the design: the design is copied as design.py beside your tests, and the failing tests are counted.

fluxpreset pytest DESIGN.py --tests test_design.py` (the design imported as `design`)
  • Run your pytest file (python-pytest, a check): fluxpreset pytest {artifact} --tests {tests} Runs your pytest file with the design importable as design; counts the failing tests. Parameters: tests ({home}/test_design.py). Reports N failing.

docs.title: accuracy
docs.text:
How far an approximation is from its reference, as a measurement, not pass or fail. max_ulp counts float64 steps.

fluxpreset accuracy DESIGN.py --call F --reference ref.py:F --random N
  • Accuracy against a reference (python-accuracy, a stage): fluxpreset accuracy {artifact} --call {call} --reference {reference} --random {random} Calls the design's function and a reference on the same cases and reports how far apart they are: absolute, relative and ULP error. Parameters: call (main), reference ({home}/reference.py), random (1000). Reports max_abs_error, mean_abs_error, max_rel_error, mean_rel_error, max_ulp.

docs.title: timebound
docs.text:
A time budget as a check: a Python function slower than --max-ms (the fastest of --runs) fails before the costly benchmark runs. A run stuck past the budget is stopped.

fluxpreset timebound DESIGN.py --call F --args "(1000,)" --max-ms 50
  • Within a time budget (python-timebound, a check): fluxpreset timebound {artifact} --call {call} --args {args} --max-ms {max_ms} Times one call of the design's function on a large input and fails a design slower than the budget, before the costly benchmark. Parameters: call (main), args (()), max_ms (1000). Reports N failing.

docs.title: bench
docs.text:
Time a Python function: the design loaded, f(*args) timed over --runs after --warmup. time_ms is the median. Exit 3 when the design does not load, 1 when it raises.

fluxpreset bench DESIGN.py --call F --args "(1000,)" [--runs 5] [--warmup 1]
  • Time a Python function (python-bench, a stage): fluxpreset bench {artifact} --call {call} --args {args} --runs {runs} Loads the design, calls one function with your arguments, times it over several runs. Parameters: call (main), args (()), runs (5). Reports time_ms.

docs.title: prog
docs.text:
Build a program with --build ({out} is the program it builds), then time, count, size or watch it. It prints name=value lines and exits 3 when the build fails. Older documents said flux prog; flux task migrate rewrites it.

fluxpreset prog time|count|memory|size --build "c++ -O2 -o {out} {artifact}" [--run CMD]
  • Program size (prog-size, a stage): fluxpreset prog size --build "{build}" Builds the program and reads its sections with size: text, data and bss bytes. Parameters: build (c++ -O2 -o {out} {artifact}). Reports text_bytes, data_bytes, bss_bytes. Needs size.
  • Program run time (prog-time, a stage): fluxpreset prog time --build "{build}" --run "{run}" --runs {runs} --warmup {warmup} Builds the program and times it over several runs (hyperfine when present). Parameters: build (c++ -O2 -o {out} {artifact}), run, runs (10), warmup (1). Reports time_ms, time_ms_stddev, time_ms_min.
  • Instruction count (Valgrind) (prog-count, a stage): fluxpreset prog count --build "{build}" --run "{run}" Builds the program and counts instructions and cache misses with Valgrind's cachegrind: deterministic. Parameters: build (c++ -O2 -o {out} {artifact}), run. Reports instructions, d1_misses, ll_misses, branch_mispredicts. Needs valgrind.
  • Program peak memory (prog-memory, a stage): fluxpreset prog memory --build "{build}" --run "{run}" --runs {runs} Builds the program and runs it: its peak resident memory as the kernel counts it, the most over the runs. Parameters: build (c++ -O2 -o {out} {artifact}), run, runs (3). Reports peak_rss_kb.

docs.title: sanitize
docs.text:
A C or C++ program built with AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer and run: each distinct memory error, leak or undefined behaviour it hits is a failure.

fluxpreset sanitize --build "cc -O1 -o {out} {artifact}" [--run CMD]
  • Memory and undefined-behaviour errors (c-sanitize, a check): fluxpreset sanitize --build "{build}" --run "{run}" Builds the program with AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer and runs it: each memory error, leak or undefined behaviour it hits is a failure. Parameters: build (cc -O1 -o {out} {artifact}), run. Reports N failing. Needs cc.

docs.title: complexity
docs.text:
How complex a design's source is, read and not run, in any common language (lizard). With --max-cyclomatic N it fails each function over N.

fluxpreset complexity DESIGN [--ext .c] [--max-cyclomatic 15]
  • Source complexity (complexity, a stage): fluxpreset complexity {artifact} Reads the design's source (any common language) and counts its lines of code, functions, cyclomatic complexity and tokens; nothing is built or run. Reports loc, functions, cyclomatic_max, cyclomatic_mean, tokens, max_function_loc.
  • No function too complex (complexity-limit, a check): fluxpreset complexity {artifact} --max-cyclomatic {max_cyclomatic} Fails each function whose cyclomatic complexity is over the limit. Parameters: max_cyclomatic (15). Reports N failing.

docs.title: scaling
docs.text:
How a command's time grows with the problem size: timed at doubling sizes ({n}; --input "gen {n}" feeds its stdin, --build makes {out} first), start-up time taken off, fitted as time ~ n^k. scaling_exponent is about 1 for linear, 2 for quadratic. With --max-exponent K it is a check.

fluxpreset scaling [--start 1000|--sizes A,B,C] [--input "gen {n}"] [--build "cc -o {out} {artifact}"] [--max-exponent K] -- CMD {n}
  • How time grows with size (scaling, a stage): fluxpreset scaling --start {start} -- {command} Times the program at doubling problem sizes and fits time ~ n^k: the exponent says how it scales (1 linear, 2 quadratic), the constant factor aside. Parameters: start (1000), command ({artifact} {n}). Reports scaling_exponent, scaling_r2, time_at_max_ms, max_n.
  • Scales no worse than n^k (scaling-limit, a check): fluxpreset scaling --start {start} --max-exponent {max_exponent} -- {command} Times the program at doubling sizes and fails when time grows faster than n to the given power. Parameters: start (1000), command ({artifact} {n}), max_exponent (1.5). Reports N failing.

docs.title: repeat
docs.text:
Any measurement run several times with its noise taken out: each metric's median and NAME_spread_pct.

fluxpreset repeat --n 5 [--warmup 1] -- CMD
  • Median of several runs (repeat, a stage): fluxpreset repeat --n {n} -- {command} Runs any measurement several times and prints each metric's median and its spread, so one noisy run does not decide. Parameters: n (5), command. Reports your name=value lines.

docs.title: derive
docs.text:
Metrics made from other metrics: a command's own numbers plus formulas over them (arithmetic, min, max, abs, sqrt, log, exp).

fluxpreset derive --expr NAME=EXPR [--expr ...] -- CMD
  • Metrics from formulas (derive, a stage): fluxpreset derive --expr {expr} -- {command} Runs any measurement and adds metrics computed from its numbers, such as area times delay or throughput per watt. Parameters: expr (adp=area_um2*path_ps), command. Reports your name=value lines.

docs.title: regress
docs.text:
A performance gate: a measurement run again and compared with a recorded baseline file. --record writes the file, --tol is the allowed percent, --higher names metrics where more is better.

fluxpreset regress --baseline base.json [--tol 5] [--record] -- CMD
  • No worse than a baseline (regress, a check): fluxpreset regress --baseline {baseline} --tol {tol} -- {command} Runs any measurement again and fails when a metric is worse than the recorded baseline by more than the tolerance. Parameters: baseline ({home}/baseline.json), tol (5), command. Reports N failing.

docs.title: extract
docs.text:
Any tool's output as name=value, so a tool that does not speak Flux needs no script: JSON, CSV or text, picked with --pick PATH=name (a dotted path, a column or a regex group).

fluxpreset extract [--format json|csv|regex] --pick PATH=name -- CMD
  • Numbers out of any tool's output (extract, a stage): fluxpreset extract --format {format} --pick {pick} -- {command} Runs your tool and reads its JSON, CSV or text output, printing the numbers you pick as name=value. Parameters: format (json), pick (value=metric), command. Reports your name=value lines.

docs.title: champsim
docs.text:
A cache prefetcher in ChampSim, on your traces. stats runs the prefetcher and the run without it on every trace and says why it wins: coverage (the share of misses removed), accuracy, lateness.

fluxpreset champsim build|check|run|stats ARTIFACT --traces DIR [--warmup N --sim N]
  • Build the prefetcher into ChampSim (champsim-build, a check): fluxpreset champsim build {artifact} Compiles a prefetcher header into ChampSim; reports the first compiler error. Reports N failing. Needs pythia.
  • Smoke-run the prefetcher (champsim-check, a check): fluxpreset champsim check {artifact} --traces {traces} Builds the prefetcher and runs it on one trace; refused when it issues no prefetches. Parameters: traces ({home}/traces). Reports N failing. Needs pythia.
  • Simulate on your traces (ChampSim) (champsim-run, a stage): fluxpreset champsim run {artifact} --traces {traces} --warmup {warmup} --sim {sim} Runs an .ini or a prefetcher header on every trace; the geometric-mean IPC speed-up over no prefetcher. Parameters: traces ({home}/traces), warmup (10000000), sim (15000000). Reports geomean_speedup. Needs pythia.
  • Why the prefetcher wins (ChampSim) (champsim-stats, a stage): fluxpreset champsim stats {artifact} --traces {traces} --warmup {warmup} --sim {sim} Runs it and the run without it on every trace: L2 misses per kilo-instruction with and without it, the share of misses it removed (coverage), and how many of its prefetches were used, late or useless. Parameters: traces ({home}/traces), warmup (10000000), sim (15000000). Reports l2_mpki, l2_mpki_baseline, pf_coverage, pf_accuracy, pf_late, pf_useless, pf_issued_pki, geomean_speedup. Needs pythia.

docs.title: asl
docs.text:
A PTO-style spec's AVS tests, from a spec checkout kept in the loop's folder. tests lists a unit's tests (by id or mnemonic); run runs them with ASLRef as the spec's release suite does, on --jobs threads, each failing test a line then N failing of M. --out FILE writes each result as JSON. Needs aslref on PATH or --aslref.

fluxpreset asl tests|run UNIT... --spec {home}/spec [--jobs N] [--out FILE]
  • The spec's AVS tests pass (asl-avs, a check): fluxpreset asl run {unit} --spec {home}/spec Runs a PTO-style spec unit's AVS tests with ASLRef, through the spec's own runner, from the spec kept in the application's folder. Each failing test a line, then the count. Parameters: unit (TADD). Reports N failing. Needs aslref.

docs.title: ndf
docs.text:
A PTO-style spec's normative clauses, read with the NDF tool. list gives each unit with its clauses by modality and its test count; clauses UNIT prints a unit's clauses; scope UNIT lists the unit and every unit that depends on it; check UNIT --results FILE reads asl run --out and counts each MUST clause failed or uncovered.

fluxpreset ndf list|clauses|scope|check UNIT --spec {home}/spec
  • Every MUST clause covered and passing (ndf-contract, a check): fluxpreset ndf check {unit} --spec {home}/spec --results {results} Reads a PTO-style spec unit's NDF clauses (the NDF tool, from the spec in the application's folder) and the AVS results fluxpreset asl run --out wrote: each MUST clause that failed or has no test is a line, then the count. Parameters: unit (TADD), results (avs.json). Reports N failing. Needs ndf.

docs.title: pto
docs.text:
A pyCircuit design checked against a PTO-style spec's ASL model, unit by unit. The design is one combinational datapath for the spec's elementwise units, with ports op (8 bits, from fluxpreset pto ops), dtype (5), a, b (64), y (64) and fault (1). Each wrong vector is a line, then N failing of M; --build-only only builds, --measure prints vectors_failing, units_passing, units. Needs pycircuit and aslref.

fluxpreset pto ops [--names]
fluxpreset pto ref UNIT...
fluxpreset pto check DESIGN --units UNIT... [--dependents] [--build-only|--measure]` (`--spec {home}/spec`)
  • The design matches the spec's ASL model (pto-check, a check): fluxpreset pto check {artifact} --units {units} --spec {home}/spec Builds a pyCircuit design (pycircuit, the C++ model) and drives it with each unit's reference vectors -- the spec's own answers from ASLRef, cached per spec -- one wrong vector a line, then the count. The interface: fluxpreset pto ops. Parameters: units (all). Reports N failing. Needs pycircuit, aslref.

docs.title: Without a preset
docs.text:
• Test script (python-test-script, a check): {python} {script} {artifact} A Python script beside the document runs the design on known cases and prints N failing. Parameters: script ({home}/check.py). Reports N failing.
  • Any command (custom-check, a check): {command} Any command; it prints N failing (or say count_re / fail_re), or its exit code decides. Parameters: command. Reports N failing.
  • Timing script (bench-script, a stage): {python} {script} {artifact} A Python script beside the document runs the design and prints time_ms=.... Parameters: script ({home}/bench.py). Reports time_ms.
  • Any command (custom-stage, a stage): {command} Any command; it prints name=value for each metric it measures, listed as the stage's metrics. Parameters: command. Reports your name=value lines.

docs.title: One interface
docs.text:
Every preset keeps the same interface:

Arguments fluxpreset NAME [SUBCOMMAND] ARTIFACT [--option VALUE ...]: the design file first, every other input an option with a default stdin Never read stdout A check: each failure on a line of its own, then N failing (or N failing of M) last. A measurement: name=value for each metric it reports stderr Diagnostics for a person; never the count or the numbers Exit code 0 passed or measured; 1 failed, or the measurement could not be taken; 2 wrong arguments; 3 the design did not build, parse or load Files Only in a temporary folder of its own; never in the loop's folder

docs.title: Writing a preset
docs.text: A preset is a module flux_presets/NAME.py (or a package) with main(argv) -> int (its command line) and catalog() -> [entry]: one catalog entry per check or stage it offers, its run starting fluxpreset NAME. flux tools, the configurator's Flux presets list and the loader's language and needs inference read those entries; nothing else in Flux names a preset.

docs.title: Golden model
docs.text:
fluxpreset golden, rtl cycles, rtl power, rtl energy and systemc read a golden model: a Python file that defines PORTS and golden(**inputs).

PORTS = [
    {"name": "x", "dir": "in", "bits": 16, "unsigned": True},
    {"name": "y", "dir": "out", "bits": 16, "unsigned": True},
]

def golden(x):
    return {"y": x}
Setting Purpose COUNT Random vectors (default 32), besides generated corner cases SEED Random seed VECTORS Extra input dictionaries; expected outputs still come from golden() EXHAUSTIVE Every input combination (at most 20 input bits) CLOCK The clock port of a clocked design, e.g. "clk" LATENCY Cycles from start to done for a clocked design TOLERANCE_ULP Map of floating-point output port to allowed ULP error; absent means exact

Match the ports and clocking in the contract and the design. Floating-point bit-pattern ports are unsigned; reinterpret their bits in golden() rather than converting the integer to a float. A Python prototype is checked against the same file with python -m flux_loop.golden_proto PROTOTYPE.py --golden golden.py (prints N failing of M).

docs.title: Common refusals
docs.text:
flux task check prints not a task: and the reason, and exits 2. The usual ones:

Message (start) Fix keys a problem document does not have: X; the keys are ... A misspelled or removed key; flux task migrate handles old ones. id is one: rename the folder instead `statement` must be a non-empty string Say what is to be made `problem.yaml` names 1 path the loop folder does not have Add the listed file to the folder, or fix the key that names it flow: X is not a box of the drawing Use one of the boxes in flow settings flow.critique is a critic on each box it judges Write critic: under orchestrate, test, measure or select (critics) flow.test is never delegated to an agent: it establishes facts test and measure are commands only flow.X: K is not a setting of this box or an agent's An option on the wrong box (agent options) flow.X: timeout_s is an agent's option, not model's Agent options need by: <agent> flow.generate is "model", {command: [...]}, {catalog: [...]} ... One form only; no timeout_s on generate flow.generate.agent.session: generate keeps one session per part Remove session from generate flow.dse is orchestrate / flow.extract is knowledge: {lessons: mined} Old names: orchestrate and knowledge.lessons flow.knowledge: who digests the papers is digest: Write knowledge: {digest: claude}, not by: ... says {x}, which is neither a knob ... nor the loop's A misspelled placeholder, or a knob not in the space flow.dse.space knobs (...) are said by no command Name a {knob} or {point} in a command, or generate with a command flow.measure.X: a command stage needs metrics ... or metrics_re Say what the stage prints roles.orchestrator: P: K is not one of its fields An option the policy does not have; the message lists its fields (search settings) a task divides into parts of ONE artifact or into subtasks ..., not both Choose one budget keys [...] are not loop knobs See budget; finalists and calibrate belong in flow flow.dse: pareto needs two objectives Add a second objective or choose another policy baseline takes file OR command OR metrics One source per baseline `problem.yaml` is not a mapping of keys The file is a list or a single value; start from flux new NAME

A missing file is listed with the key that names it and what the folder holds. A refused document never runs; flux task check FOLDER shows the same message before you start.

docs.title: Search policies
docs.text: What flow.orchestrate takes as a search. Search and agents explains when to use which.

docs.title: Space and seeds
docs.text:
A search tries points of a space of settings ("knobs"). flow.orchestrate is a search when it is a policy name, a list of phases, or a map with policy, space or seeds:

orchestrate:
  policy: {gradient: {steps: 16, patience: 2}}     # or: policy: gradient
  space:
    algorithm: [list_sieve, slice_sieve, odd_sieve]
    wheel: {values: [0, 1], when: {algorithm: [list_sieve]}}   # only moves for list_sieve
    prefetch:                                       # a component: prefetch.on, .distance, .degree
      optional: true
      distance: [1, 2, 4]
      degree: [1, 2]
    variant: {values: [baseline], from: "variants/*.py"}       # plus file stems found at load
  seeds:
    - {algorithm: list_sieve, wheel: 0}            # measured first; the first seed is home
  • space: knob to an ordered, non-empty list of scalar choices. A map with values takes when: {knob: choice or [choices]} (the knob only moves when the condition holds; otherwise it sits at its first choice) and from: glob (adds the stems of matching files, relative to the folder, read at every load). A map with neither is a component: its knobs are named component.knob; optional: true adds component.on. Order numeric choices: local policies step to neighbours.
  • seeds: points measured first; a missing knob takes its first choice.
  • A space must reach a command: some command names a {knob} or {point}, or the generator is a command or a catalog. A model or agent generator with a space searches settings only and does not write designs.
  • Component knobs reach commands through {point} only; {component.knob} is not substituted.

docs.title: Policies
docs.text: Policy Options and defaults sweep batch_size: 0 (the whole walk at once) montecarlo samples: 24, batch_size: 8, seed: 0 gradient steps: 16, wave: 0 (all moves), patience: 1, budget: 0 (no cap), reach: adjacent (or any) anneal steps: 32, seed: 0, temperature: 1.0, cooling: 0.9 genetic population: 8, generations: 6, seed: 0, mutation: 0.3 pareto budget: 24, wave: 6, reference: [], scale: [], reach: adjacent; needs two objectives flux FluxAgent proposing points: batch_size: 4, rounds: 8, shown: 40; written {by: flux, ...} (model, its old name, too) or {by: claude, ...} for an agent control keep: []: compare home with only these incumbent knobs kept phases phases: [...]: phases in order, each {policy: ..., ...its options} (default gradient); phases do not nest adaptive, explore, improve, tune, finetune, variations FluxAgent proposing points with that emphasis (flux's options) command Your own search: orchestrate: {command: ..., timeout_s: 600} (contract)

docs.title: Options every policy takes
docs.text:
Every policy and phase also takes name (a label), knobs (move only these), hold (keep these fixed; both accept globs such as prefetch.*), metric and direction (its own target; default the first objective), floor ({metric, at} or {metric, keep, above}: designs below it are refused), margin (minimum improvement, default 0) and dse (an emphasis, as above). batch is another name for batch_size. An unknown option is refused, naming the policy's fields.

A policy's batch_size only groups its proposals. budget.batch is how many search designs one pass carries; budget.parallel is how many passes run at once. Finishing a finite walk does not stop an open-ended run: cap it with budget.passes.

docs.title: Write a loop with an agent
docs.text: Describe what you want, give it your files, and let an author write the loop: the document, its checks and measurements, and a golden model where one fits. The author is FluxAgent or a coding agent. You review what it wrote, then run it.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
flux ask "a signed 8x8 multiplier in SystemVerilog, the smallest that makes 1 GHz placed on ASAP7" \
  --file spec.pdf --author claude --no-run

The author writes the loop into ./out/ask_<slug>/ (--dir DIR to choose; the folder's name is the loop's id). It runs flux task check on its own draft and repairs what the check refuses, up to --checks times (default 3). An agent author also writes decisions.json: each decision it took and a one-line reason.

Without --no-run, the loop then runs: after each pass the author reads the report and may revise the document. --passes N caps the run; without it the run goes on until you stop it. flux ask --tui (or no prompt) opens a setup screen for the prompt, files, author and passes.

Option Effect --file PATH An input: a spec, code, a reference, a PDF, tests (repeatable; a folder is copied whole) --author WHO flux (FluxAgent, the default; model is the same), claude, codex, opencode, or an agent of your own --hidden PATH A path in the loop hidden from AI: the author and the loop's agents may not read it (repeatable) --skill DIR A skill folder for the author and the designers (repeatable) --questions operator Let an agent author ask you a question, answered within --wait-s seconds (default 600) --no-run Write and check the loop; run nothing --repair The loop in --dir was refused: check it and repair it, writing nothing new (--note says what to do)

The author gets the skills flux-loop-creator and flux-loop-commands, and reads the bundled loops in flux/applications/ for reference. See the CLI for every option.

docs.title: In the web app
docs.text:
New loop › Agent walks through four stages:

  1. Ask: the loop's name, the agent, what the loop should do, and the files it should read. Mark a file Hide from AI to keep it from every agent (a gate's tests, for example). Ask me when unclear lets the agent ask you questions.
  2. Drafting: its work as lines, what it read, wrote and ran. A question shows inline with its choices as buttons, a free answer, or You decide. If its check refuses the draft, Try again sends it another round, or write a note telling it what to do.
  3. Review: its decisions, grouped by the configurator's steps, each with its reason. Keep one, Change it in the configurator at that step, or Keep the rest. A change asked of the agent shows as a diff on the document.
  4. Ready: flux task check on the draft. Run one cheap pass first runs one pass that stops at the first measurement. Make loop, or Open in configurator to edit it first.

The draft exists as a loop from Drafting on; this browser remembers it, so you can come back. A loop's Settings › Problem › Agent asks an agent to change an existing loop the same way.

docs.title: Check what it wrote
docs.text:
An author's loop is a first draft. Before a long run:

  • Read the checks: do they test what you care about, on enough inputs?
  • Read the measurements: the right workload, the right stage, workers: 1 for timings?
  • Read the objectives: the limit you meant, in the right direction?
  • Run one pass (flux task run FOLDER --passes 1) and read the report.

Configure explains each part of the document, and Knowledge, skills, hidden paths what the agents read.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: Flux is a Python package. The command line needs Python 3.11 or newer; the web app, the hardware tools and the sandbox are optional extras.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
The Flux source is not public: ask its maintainer for access. Then, from its folder (here flux-repo):

cd flux-repo
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -e ./flux
source .venv/bin/activate
flux selftest --no-model

flux selftest checks this machine: a script-driven loop, the tools on PATH, and, without --no-model, the model endpoint and a coding agent. It prints PASS, FAIL or SKIP per check.

docs.title: Sandbox
docs.text:
flux task check, flux task run and flux ask run inside a container, so a loop's code and its agents cannot touch the rest of your machine. Install Podman (rootless, preferred) or Docker. Without either, these commands stop with the sandbox needs Podman or Docker.

For code you trust, such as the first loop, run on your machine directly:

export FLUX_SANDBOX=0        # or --no-sandbox on each command

What the sandbox sees, writes and reaches is in Run, stop, resume.

docs.title: Web app
docs.text:
pip install -e "./flux[web]"
flux user add me --admin
flux serve

Run flux user add as the user who should own the loops' files. flux serve prints its address (by default http://127.0.0.1:8765/); open it and sign in. The Web app pages walk through it, and Server and admin covers running it for a team.

docs.title: Hardware tools
docs.text:
