Loops that synthesise, place or simulate hardware need Verilator, Yosys, OpenROAD and the other packaged tools. They come with Flux's Nix development shell. Install Nix and enable experimental-features = nix-command flakes in ~/.config/nix/nix.conf, then:

cd flux
nix develop --accept-flake-config
flux selftest --no-model

The first entry may build or download tools. The shell also carries the coding agents Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode (Models and agents). The shell puts Flux itself on PATH; no pip install is needed inside it. Keep your loop folders wherever you like and pass their paths to Flux.

docs.title: Models and agents
docs.text: A loop whose designs come from a script needs no model. For a model or a coding agent, see Models and agents.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• First loop: a complete loop from an empty folder, in Python only.
  • Loop crafter: build the document in your browser.
  • Write a loop with an agent: describe what you want and let an agent write the loop.

docs.title: Tour
docs.text: flux serve is a shared server with accounts. Each user has loops; each loop is a document and its files, and runs on the server, sandboxed. You check, start and stop loops, follow them live, and read their results in the browser. Install starts one.

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
The first page lists your loops: their state, how many designs were accepted and measured, and the decision's number on the first objective (✓ or ✗ against its limit). Search, filter by state, and sort by activity, name or decision. Shared with me lists loops others shared with you or your group, with what you may do in a few words ("ask · edit · run"). Archived loops are under their own Archived chip (Archive).

When you see a group's project, a row of project chips sits under the state chips: All projects, one per group project (a project with no loop yet shows a muted 0; choosing it says "No loops yet" with a link to the project, where you link one), and Not in a project. The list stays flat, each loop once: its group projects are small tags under its name (a link to the project), "+ global" when it is in a global project too, and a loop of someone else's that you reach through a project says "via" that project (Groups).

docs.title: New loop
docs.text:
New loop offers five ways to make one:

Way What it does Configurator A form in six steps, the same as the Loop crafter Create or upload An empty loop, or one from a folder, files or a .zip you drop or pick, or from a problem document pasted (Paste YAML) Direct edit Write the YAML yourself Agent An agent writes the loop from your prompt and files (Write a loop with an agent) Clone A copy of an existing loop, with its problem but none of its runs

docs.title: A loop's page
docs.text:
A loop has six tabs, and its run buttons in its header: Start (▶) at rest, Stop (■) and Restart (↻) joined while it runs, each with its word, beside the header's other buttons. The same buttons are at the end of each row of the Loops list as small square icons; hover one (or focus it) for what it does.

Tab What it shows Overview Its state, the decision against the limits, the best designs, a best-so-far chart, the last pass Live What the run does now, as a tree, a graph, a timeline or the log (Live) Results Every design measured, charts, ideas and the library (Results) Agents Every model and agent turn: where it was taken (pass, box, try) and how its try came out, prompt, reply, tool calls, time and tokens Files The loop's files and the agents' workbench (Files and settings) Settings Preferences, sharing, maintenance, and the problem itself (Files and settings)

Start asks for the passes (or "until I stop it") and whether to stop at the first measurement. It runs flux task check first when the inputs changed; if the check fails, the button reads Start anyway. A start resumes from the record. A failed loop's Start says Start again; while an agent is still writing the problem, Start waits.

Stop and Restart take effect after the current pass. Once one is asked, only that button is tinted red, with a small hourglass (after its word in the header, in its corner in a row), and the page says when it happens ("Stops after pass 4."). The other button still works, so a stop can become a restart and back. Hover or focus the tinted button and it turns solid red: press it again to do it now. It asks first, then abandons the pass, and the button stays solid red until the process ends.

docs.title: A loop's Chat
docs.text:
Chat, on every tab of a loop, opens a panel of conversations about the loop (it was called Talk before; old #/app/NAME/ask and #/app/NAME/talk links still open it, and #/app/NAME/chat/ID opens one conversation). Ask puts a question (why it stalls, which design is best, what to try next) to an agent or FluxAgent, which reads the document, the files, the record and the log, and changes nothing. It is told the loop's baseline and how far the best design and the standing pick are from it, and an agent reads the record with flux loop summary, passes, results, tried and show before any query of its own (CLI). Thinking & commands under an answer shows how it was made: an agent's work, or the queries FluxAgent ran. While the loop runs, a note you send there reaches its next prompt, or answers an agent's open question. In the message box Enter sends and Shift+Enter starts a new line.

Chat, in the top bar, is the same kind of conversation bound to no loop: it may read all your loops and keep tools and notes in your workbench (Chat). Its list also folds each loop's conversations under Loop chats, so you can open and continue them there (Loop chats).

docs.title: Everywhere
docs.text:
• Top bar: Chat · Loops · Groups · Admin (admins only). Groups shows your groups, their members and projects, and the global projects (Groups). These pages, and your Account, start with their content, not a title that repeats the bar: New loop is at the end of the Loops list's search bar (or in the empty list), Admin's tabs and Groups' tabs are at the top.
  • Theme: system, light or dark, from the top bar; remembered in this browser.
  • Bell: a run ends or fails, an agent asks a question, a loop is shared with you.
  • Raw and Fullscreen on files, logs, results and agent turns.
  • Addresses name the view, so a link opens it: #/app/NAME/live/log, #/app/NAME/settings/problem?step=graph.
  • On a phone the account items move to the ☰ menu, and lists and tabs stack; on a narrow one the bar's links draw smaller so all four fit beside the bell and ☰.

The Preview app runs the same pages in your browser on sample data.

docs.title: Run a server
docs.text:
flux user add ada --admin       # the first account, on the server's machine
flux serve                      # http://127.0.0.1:8765/
Option Effect --host HOST, --port PORT Where it listens (default 127.0.0.1:8765); put a TLS proxy in front for others --secure-cookie Send the session cookie over HTTPS only, behind a TLS proxy --data DIR The server's data (default $XDG_DATA_HOME/flux/web): accounts, keys, every user's loops --max-running N Runs at once per user --no-sandbox Runs on the host, not sandboxed: for a single trusted user only

flux user add and flux serve must name the same data folder; both print it. Run them as the user who should own the loops' files.

  • Data: the data folder holds flux-web.db, secret.key (which encrypts keys and secrets) and every user's loops under users/<name>/apps/. Back up flux-web.db and secret.key together (Admin › Maintenance can) and the loop folders separately.
  • Limits: a loop holds up to 100,000 files and 8 GB; one upload, 900 files and 256 MB.
  • Restarts: a restarted server finds its running loops again; their containers keep running while it is down. scripts/install-service.py (from flux/) installs it as a user service that restarts only the server on updates, or as a system service (User or system service).
  • Slow requests (over 0.5 s; FLUX_SLOW_S sets it) are logged as flux serve: slow: ....
  • Before a login the server serves only the sign-in page (/login: the login, and the invitation and reset links, /#/invite/...) and the few files it loads; / sends a browser there, and every other page, script and stylesheet of the app answers 404 until there is a session, checked on each request (a logout ends it at once). The app's files are sent Cache-Control: private, so a shared cache or proxy keeps none of them. The docs' Preview is not covered: it runs the whole app in the browser, by design (minified, and sealed behind its passphrase on the published site).

docs.title: Loops from the server's machine
docs.text:
flux web-loop lists, starts, stops and reads the web's loops from a shell on the server's machine. It never runs a loop itself: it asks the running server, which starts and stops the run as its Start and Stop buttons do, with the same limits, pause, checks, audit and live pages.

flux web-loop ls                          # every loop: owner/loop, state, last start, the agents its problem names
flux web-loop ls --user cedric
flux web-loop start cedric/nlu            # as the Start dialog: the last start's passes, else 1
flux web-loop start cedric/nlu --forever  # until stopped; --passes N, --screen-only, --document F, --rerun-baseline
flux web-loop status cedric/nlu           # running pass N or idle, the last start, the log's last lines (--lines N)
flux web-loop stop cedric/nlu             # at the end of the pass; --now abandons it

A loop is USER/LOOP, its owner first. Each request acts as the loop's owner: the run is theirs, on their running limit, and each audit line it writes ends "(by host)". The agents and models are the loop's problem's (its flow, Settings › Problem); a start takes only what the Start dialog takes. --json prints the server's answer; --data names the data folder, as for flux user.

The server listens for it on a unix socket in the account's runtime folder, $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/flux/control-<hash>.sock (one per data folder; <data>/.server/control.sock when there is no runtime folder), mode 0600, owned by the server's account; it is made each time flux serve starts (a socket left by a server that ended is replaced) and removed when it stops. With no server answering there, flux web-loop says the server is not running. The trust boundary is the data folder: whoever can open the socket can already read and change every account and loop in that folder, so is the server's admin; run flux web-loop as the account that runs flux serve.

docs.title: Agents' Tests from the server's machine
docs.text:
A start waits for each agent its problem names to have passed its Test for the loop's owner, of the configuration as it is now ("Codex not set up for cedric yet (its configuration changed since its Test)"). A new program for an agent (a Codex update) is a new configuration: every user who uses it needs a new Test. flux web-agent runs that Test for them, through the running server, as flux web-loop does:

flux web-agent ls                         # each user's agents: ready, or needs Test and why; the last Test
flux web-agent ls codex --user cedric
flux web-agent test                       # every user, each agent they set up: one line each, ok or failed, its seconds
flux web-agent test codex --needed        # only those whose gate is not ready; --jobs 2 for two at once
flux web-agent test codex --user cedric   # one user (an agent named: tested even if never set up)
flux web-agent test codex --loop cedric/nlu   # in that loop's context, its variables

It is the same Test as Account › Agents' button: the server runs it in the user's own home with their own settings, variables and sandbox, and keeps the result as theirs; flux web-agent sees no credential. "Set up" is logged in, or tested before (the admin's Test of the server's configuration counts too); a disabled user is skipped unless named. The loops whose own variables run an agent otherwise, and that were tested in their context, are tested again in it. A Test ends by itself after 420 s and says why; a failed one says what the page says and makes the exit 1. Each Test is on the audit as the user's "agent test", ending "(by host)".

docs.title: Accounts
docs.text:
flux user manages accounts from the server's machine:

flux user add bob --invite --url https://flux.example   # a link for bob to choose a password
flux user list
flux user role bob admin
flux user link bob                                      # a password reset link
flux user rename bob robert                             # everything of bob's, re-keyed
flux user delete robert --transfer-to cy                # robert gone, his loops cy's (or --delete-loops)

A link works once, for a week; there is no mail. In the app, Admin › Users does the same: a row per user with the Admin, Create and Run boxes, a Limits cell (how many of their loops run at once, empty for the server's default, and an Active switch: off disables the account, after asking), their groups as pills (× leaves one, + searches the others), Last active, their usage behind Show usage, and a ⋯ menu with View as (the app as they see it, read-only), a reset or invitation link, Rename… and Delete… (Deletes). Headers sort, and the order is remembered. flux user role bob admin makes bob an admin; user takes the flag away.

A new password logs the user out everywhere: one set from a link, by flux user passwd or by an admin in the app ends all their sessions (for the last two, a notice tells the user at their next login); one changed on their own Account ends all but the session that changed it.

  • Admin is the user's own. An admin administers the server and may do anything with every loop. An admin cannot clear their own Admin box; an admin has Create and Run.
  • Credentials are a group's. Each group is set to Server settings (runs use the server's model, agent and variable settings beneath the user's own) or Own settings (members bring their own settings and agent logins). A user gets the server's settings when any of their groups gives them; in no such group, or in no group at all, they use their own. Admins follow the same rule. A new group starts with own settings. Your Account names the group that gives you the server's settings; Groups in the top bar shows it per group (Groups).
  • Groups: a user is in no group, one or several. Admin › Users › Groups lists each group with its member count, its Credentials, their Effect (who gets the server's settings through it, or through another group), Open projects give (the level its open projects give its members unless a project says another; Asker by default), Rename… and Delete…. A group unrolls to the member grid under its name: a row per member with a Level (see the words), the Member column every member has, a box per word (hover a column's name for its meaning) and × to remove them. The All members row on top gives a word to everyone or takes it from everyone (a dash: some have it). + Add people is under the table; a new member starts as Member. On a phone a member is a block: the name and ×, the level, then the words three to a line. A project's members and a loop's Sharing are the same grid.
  • Permissions of the account, whatever the groups: Create loops and Run loops and agents. A user in no group still creates and runs their own loops.
  • A membership's words -- curate, manage, create (Member, Maintainer, Lead) -- act on the group's projects, never on a loop: being in a group gives nothing on any loop (see the words).
  • Archive, reset, delete, rename and transfer stay with the owner and the admins. A loop is reached in two ways only: its owner (or one with share on it) shares it with a user or a group, or links it into a project. What someone may do with it is the union of their row, their groups' rows and what the projects it is linked into give them. Ask and Run also need Run loops and agents.

docs.title: The words
docs.text:
One vocabulary for loops, groups and projects (GET /api/words serves it): the loop words view, ask, edit, run act on loops -- one shared loop, or the loops linked into a project; share is a loop's own (whoever holds it chooses who else gets the loop, giving at most what they hold). The place words act on a group or a project: link (link one's own loops into a project), curate (review a project's knowledge, keep its library), manage (members, levels, access, title; rename, archive, delete) and, on a group only, create (make projects; the maker is the project's Lead).

A loop is reached in two ways only: a share (to the person, or to a group of theirs), or being in a project it is linked into -- one of its members, with their level there, or a member of its group when the project opens to the group. A group membership carries no loop word: being in a group gives nothing on any loop by itself.

Place Words Loop share view · ask · edit · run · share Group membership curate · manage · create Project level view · ask · edit · run · link · curate · manage Global project level curate · manage

Levels are one ladder in every place, cut to each place's words; a mix that matches no level reads Custom:

Level Words Loop Project Group Global project Member none -- yes yes yes Viewer view yes yes -- -- Asker view · ask yes yes -- -- Contributor view · ask · edit · run · link yes (no link) yes -- -- Maintainer Contributor and curate, create (on a loop: view · ask · edit · run · share) yes yes curate · create curate Lead every word -- yes curate · manage · create curate · manage

A loop's levels stop at Maintainer; its Owner row is shown, never given. A word that acts on a loop brings view with it.

Why a place has no box for a word (the grids leave these out):

Place Word Why not Loop share link covered by share: linking needs share on the loop (its owner has it) and link on the project Loop share curate a loop's record is not curated: what it teaches reaches a project's curators Loop share manage its owner's only (rename, transfer, archive, delete): the Owner row, never given Loop share create loops are made on the account (Create loops) Group membership view, ask, edit, run a loop is reached through a share or a project one is in, never a membership Group membership link linking is a project's word: its members' level, or its open level Group membership share a loop's own: a group never shares its members' loops onward Project level share a loop's own: a link is consent to the project only Project level create projects do not nest Global project level view its visibility gives it: everyone a public one, its members a private one Global project level ask, edit, run, link a global project gives nobody a word on its loops; who links is its join rule

Who manages a group or a project gives anyone a level or words up to their own there; admins any. The open levels are set by the group's managers (a membership has no loop word to bound them) and by a project's own managers within their words.

What a group gives. On the loops linked into its projects, only what each project's group access says: invite (the default for a new project) gives nothing on its loops and is private: hidden from the group's members until they are added (its managers and curators see it); view gives every member view on it and its loops; open gives every member the project's open level (the group's default, Asker unless set, or the project's own) -- that level, nothing more. Its words reach every project of the group, whatever its access: curate curates them, manage manages them and the group's members, create makes projects.

Global projects. A global project is public (everyone sees it, its library and its knowledge) or private (only the members an admin or its managers add, and admins, see it; elsewhere it is not found). Its members hold only curate or manage (Member, Maintainer, Lead). Nobody sees another person's loops linked into it but admins and its managers; in a private one its members do not see the other members either. Who links loops into it is its join rule (everyone, or admins), and in a private one only its members. There is no curator group: a curator is a member with curate.

docs.title: Renames
docs.text:
Only an admin renames a user: Admin › Users, the row's ⋯ › Rename… (or flux user rename). Everything that holds the name moves with it -- the user's folder (loops, chats, home), their sandbox caches, their loops' settings, variables, shares and result columns, the shares other owners gave them, their runs' paths, scheduled changes naming them, chats that focus on their loops, the questions they asked, their usage. It is refused while anything of theirs works: a run of their loops, an agent writing or answering about one, a chat answer, a login or an agent test. There are no redirects: links to the old name stop working, so everyone their loops are shared with is told once, with the new link, and so is the user. Their sessions stay; they log in with the new name from then on. The audit keeps the old name where it was written, with one "rename user" entry.

Admin › Users › Groups › Rename… renames a group; its members, their permissions and its shares stay (they are kept by the group's id), and its members are told. Names are one whatever their case; _ is reserved and / is not allowed (a project is addressed <group>/<name>).

docs.title: Deletes
docs.text:
Active off (in Limits) disables a user: logged out, unable to log in, everything kept. ⋯ › Delete… is the hard one, for admins only. Its dialog says what the user holds -- their loops (and whom each is shared with), the projects only they manage, the loops shared with them, their groups and sessions -- and asks where their loops go: transferred to another user (each moves as a transfer does, with its files, record, runs and projects; its shares cleared; a name the other user already has becomes <loop>-<user>, shown before you confirm) or deleted (as the loop's own Delete). Then their account goes with everything kept for them: sessions, invites, notifications, memberships, project levels, the shares to them, their own model settings, variables and agents' keys, their Overview layout, scheduled changes for them, their folder (chats, home, agents' logins) and sandbox caches. The audit keeps their name where it was written, with one "delete user" entry; the usage log, transcripts and others' chats stay as history. It is refused while a loop of theirs runs or anything of theirs works (as a rename), for yourself and for the last enabled admin; you type their name to confirm. Whom their loops were shared with is told, and so is the user who got them. flux user delete NAME --transfer-to USER (or --delete-loops) does the same from the server's machine.

Groups › Delete… is refused while the group has a project, archived ones too: the dialog lists them, each a link to its page to delete it. Otherwise it says the members, the loops shared with the group and, first, the members who get the server's settings through this group alone: they change to their own. You type its name to confirm; its memberships, the loop shares made to it and its settings go, and its members are told. Its members keep their accounts and loops.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text:
Think of a group as an organisation and a project as one of its repositories: the project has its own members, and loops are linked into it. A project belongs to one group, addressed <group>/<name>, or is global, addressed _/<name> and shown "global / …". Names are letters, digits, - and _, one per group whatever their case; titles are free. The Groups page lists a group's projects and makes new ones, and each project has a page of its own: its loops and its members. The API (/api/projects, /api/groups/mine) and flux project on the server's machine manage them:

flux project create hw/nlu --title "NLU operators"                    # --access invite|view|open (invite)
flux project create _/techniques --visibility private --join admins  # global: admins only (public by default)
flux project member _/techniques cy maintainer                        # a global project's: member, maintainer (curate) or lead (curate, manage)
flux project access _/techniques public                               # a global project's visibility: public or private
flux project member hw/nlu bob contributor                            # a level, or view,ask,link ... or none (a Member)
flux project member hw/nlu bob remove
flux project access hw/nlu open viewer                                # what the group's members get: open, at Viewer (group: the group's)
flux project rename hw/nlu nlu-ops                                    # the old address stops working
flux project archive hw/nlu-ops                                       # --undo unarchives
flux project list --all
flux project delete hw/nlu-ops --yes

Levels are the words' ladder cut to a project's words (view, ask, edit, run, link, curate, manage); the one who makes a project is its Lead. A Member (no words) sees the project and its members, nothing more. Group access, per project, says what the group's members get without being its members: invite (private: hidden from them until they are added, but for the members whose group membership curates or manages; the default for a new project), view (they view it and its loops; every project made before reads so) or open (each gets its open level, nothing more). There is no joining: a project's own members are added by those who manage it; anyone may leave a project.

What someone may do with a project is the union of: what its group access gives, their membership of its group (curate and manage on every project of the group), their own level as its member, and a global project's view (everyone a public one, its members a private one). Rights only add up: nobody loses a right because of a project. Admins may do everything. Members with create make the group's projects; only admins make global ones and choose whether each is public or private and who may link loops into them; a global project's members (curate or manage) are added by admins and its managers. Archiving hides a project from the lists and freezes it until it is unarchived. Every change is in the audit.

Admin › Users › Projects lists every project, the groups' and the global ones, archived ones too: its title (a link to its page) and address, its group, how many loops are linked into it, how many members it has and the size of its library. A global project's Visibility (Public or Private) and Who links loops (everyone, admins only) are set in its row; each row's ⋯ opens it, renames it, archives or unarchives it, deletes it. New global project is under the list. GET /api/admin/projects answers the list.

A project's library (<data>/projects/<group-id>/<name>/library/, written only by the server) is browsed and changed from its page as a loop's files are, through /api/projects/<group>/<name>/library (what it holds, what one may do), .../library/files, .../file (GET, PUT, DELETE), .../item, .../item/size, .../move, POST .../files, PUT/DELETE .../part and .../hidden. View browses; edit, curate or manage changes; manage hides paths from the agents (kept on the project, in the database and its project.json). Paths stay inside it, links are never followed or made, a zip holding a link is refused; it holds what a loop may (100,000 files, 8 GB). No loop reads it yet.

docs.title: Loops in projects
docs.text:
A loop is in no project, one or several, in an order its owner sets. Linking a loop is its owner's consent; the project's roles then decide. Only its owner (or an admin) links it: into a group's project where they hold link, or into a global project (anyone -- a private one's members only -- unless its join rule is admins); an archived project takes none.

  • On every loop linked into a group's project, each of its members gets their roles' loop words -- view, ask, edit, run -- and the group's members what its access gives (view, or the open level). This adds to what shares give, never takes away (a group membership gives no loop word); ask and run still need the account's Run loops and agents; curate, link and manage stay the project's. An archived project gives none until unarchived.
  • A global project gives nobody any right on a loop. A user sees only their own loops in it; admins and its managers see every one.
  • Each link keeps an extraction consent: whether what its runs teach may be extracted for the project's knowledge (kept for when extraction comes). On by default for a group's project, the owner's to switch; off for a global one, where only an admin or one of its managers turns it on and the owner may turn it off.

A loop renamed or transferred keeps its projects; a loop deleted leaves them; a project deleted lets its loops go and tells their owners. The API is GET /api/apps/<loop>/projects?owner=<owner> and PUT the same path with the whole ordered list, [{"project": "hw/nlu", "extract": true}] (left out, extract keeps what it was, or the default); POST /api/projects/<group>/<name>/loops links one of one's loops, PUT and DELETE on .../loops/<owner>/<loop> change its learning or take it out; each project in /api/projects lists its loops, and each loop in the loop lists its projects. On the server's machine:

flux project loop bob/adder                          # its projects, in order
flux project loop bob/adder set hw/nlu _/techniques  # exactly these, in this order (none: no project)
flux project loop bob/adder add hw/dsp               # one more, last
flux project loop bob/adder extract hw/nlu off
flux project loop bob/adder remove hw/dsp
flux project loops hw/nlu                            # the project's loops

docs.title: Your account
docs.text:
Account holds your Agents (each agent's login, Test, model and variables), your usage, your password, desktop notifications, and the Overview layout used on every loop; a line names your groups and links to the Groups page. Changing the password asks for the current one (wrong ones count and lock as a login's do) and logs out your other sessions.

An agent is used only once its Test passed for whoever starts the loop. A login runs the agent's own login command in the sandbox, in a small terminal; Claude Code's token is stored encrypted and never shown again. An agent never runs on FluxAgent: without settings of its own, it uses its own configuration and login (Models and agents).

docs.title: Admin
docs.text:
Tab What it holds Loops Every user's loops (a loop is archived from its own settings); pause new starts, stop or restart them all after their pass; documents of an earlier form, with Migrate all Insights Failed starts and agent Tests, usage and cost by user and agent (the knowledge collector's calls as their loop's), endpoints, refused hosts, the audit trail Resources CPUs, memory and disks over time, the sandbox containers, each loop's disk and caches Maintenance Scheduled clean-up tasks, each on or off, with Run now; scheduled changes of a setting Sandbox Limits (CPUs, memory, processes, scratch: a default and a maximum), the network (open, or an allowlist), the PATH directories mounted, what every user's home starts with Agents FluxAgent and each agent: program, login, model and key, seconds per turn, token prices, whether Ask may use it, thinking by default; + Add agent Chat What users may use in Chat (the tab, network beyond the base allowlist, the workbench, loop access), the hosts a chat may also reach, overrides per group and user (Chat) Users Users, groups and permissions, invitations, View as; Projects: every project

Keys are stored encrypted and never shown again. With nothing set, runs use the machine's own configuration (~/.config/flux/flux.env, and each agent's own).

docs.title: Thinking by default
docs.text:
Each agent's panel in Admin › Agents, and FluxAgent's, says whether it Thinks by default: where a loop's box does not say (think: beside by: flux or an agent, an agent's effort:, Thinking) and as the Think switch of a chat's composer starts for it (Chat). An agent also has the effort it works at when thinking and when not, from the levels its kind takes (Claude Code --effort, Codex model_reasoning_effort, OpenCode --variant); its own adds no flag. FluxAgent has its own four efforts -- low, medium, high, max: thinking, tool rounds and answer length at once (Chat); built in is high thinking and medium not.

Thinks by default Effort when thinking when not Each agent on its own (no flag) its kind's lowest (low, or minimal) FluxAgent off built in (high) built in (medium)

Untouched, loops run exactly as they did: agents with no effort flag, FluxAgent answering straight. A loop's box worked by FluxAgent takes an effort only when one is said: its effort:, or one picked here -- the built-in levels leave its requests (its tool turns, its output) as they were. What wins, first to last: a chat's Think, the loop's box, this default. Saved at once and audited (thinking by default); a run, a chat or an ask started afterwards takes it.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text: Sandbox containers lists every container the sandbox runs, read every 15 seconds, with its CPU, memory and processes. Whose says what each one is: a loop's (its link; Stop ends the loop after its pass, View opens the loop whose author or Talk uses it), Chat · user (a user's chat sandbox; kept when it stays between answers, each answer running in it named under it), Login · user or Agent test · user. Its state says answering or kept, idle for a chat's. Stop on a chat's stops the answers running in it, each saying it was stopped, and removes it: the user's next message starts a fresh one. A container no process runs any more is left behind, with Kill; the scheduled clean-up removes those itself, never one a loop, a login, a test or a chat still uses.

docs.title: Maintenance
docs.text:
The scheduled tasks clean scratch and leftover containers, compact the databases, condense run logs, prune old records and agent folders, alert when a disk fills, and back up the server's database. Bring task journals up to date converts journals written by an older Flux, so Live can read them. Three tasks act on a loop's record, off the schedule by default and run on one loop: Invalidate all sets every design aside (shown, re-measure pending, never chosen), Re-Evaluate asks the loop's next start to measure the pending designs again (its boxes add pass 0, the failed designs, or every design), and Show hidden evaluations shows again what an older Flux's invalidation hid, on one loop or every loop at rest (see Results). Running loops are never touched, archived loops only by the checks, compaction and journal updates, and every run is audited.

Maintenance has three tabs, each with a filter box and chips that narrow its rows:

Tab What it lists Tasks The built-in tasks: running first, then queued, failed, done and off. Chips: Running, Queued, Failed, Off Scheduled changes Your scheduled changes (below), soonest next run first. A chip per setting or kind History Every run of a task or a change, newest first: what, when, by whom (the schedule, the server's start-up, or an admin's Run now), how long it took and its result. Chips: Failed, Scheduled changes, Run now. The last 1000 runs are kept

On a phone each row is two or three lines: its name with its buttons, then its schedule and last run, then its result.

One task runs at a time. Run now (the ▶ button on each row; on every loop, or on one) runs the task at once when nothing else runs; otherwise it joins a queue, first come first run, and the row says queued · 2nd with Cancel. Asking again for a task already queued or running adds nothing. Scheduled runs join the same queue. A running task shows a spinner and how long it has run. The queue lives in the server's memory: a restart drops it, and the schedule asks again. Resetting, renaming, transferring or archiving a loop is still refused while a task runs, never between two.

A task runs every so many minutes, hours or days, or daily at a time on the days picked, or on a cron expression (the same form as a scheduled change's, below). A task at a time of day runs once when its time comes; a time already past when it is set waits for its next day.

docs.title: Scheduled changes
docs.text:
A scheduled change does one thing at a time of day. + Scheduled change asks first for its kind, then that kind's fields, then when:

Kind What it does Turns at once Sets one endpoint limit: turns at once of an agent's endpoint, or requests at once of FluxAgent (the limits under Admin › Agents), checked as that form checks it: a whole number, 0 for no limit Pause starts Pauses new starts with a reason (up to 200 characters), or resumes them. Running loops go on. While paused, starts, owners' restarts, Restart all and a pending restart after a pass are refused with the reason Running limit A user's running-loops limit (0–64, or default), or the server's default (0–64, or default: the --max-running flag). New starts only Stop loops Stops the running loops after their pass: every loop, one user's, or one loop. Now (off by default) stops them at once, the current pass abandoned Start a loop Starts one loop as its owner, with the options of its last start, for 1–1000 passes or until stopped. Refused, and shown as a failed run, when the loop is gone or archived, its owner is disabled or may not run loops, starts are paused, the owner is at their limit, or it already runs

When is daily at a time on the days picked, or, under Advanced: cron expression, five cron fields: minute, hour, day of the month, month, day of the week. */15 9-17 * * 1-5 means every 15 minutes from 09:00 to 17:59 on weekdays. The form says the schedule in words and its next times. Times are the server's own, and its time zone is shown beside the field.

For example, to leave the shared endpoint to people by day and give it to the loops by night, add two changes to Claude Code's turns at once:

Change When Claude Code turns at once → 1 daily at 08:00, Mon–Fri Claude Code turns at once → 4 daily at 20:00, every day

A night of runs, for example, takes three changes, every day: Start a loop at 20:00 until stopped, Pause starts at 20:05 with the reason nightly runs (no one else starts one), and Stop loops at 07:00, every loop after its pass, with Pause starts set to Resume starts at 07:30.

Each change is a row with its schedule, next run, last run and result, Run now (▶, queued like any task), and Edit…, Turn off/Turn on and Delete… in its menu. A change takes effect at the next turn of every loop, running loops too. Lowering the limit stops no running turn: running turns finish, and new turns wait until fewer than the new limit run.

A stop or a start happens at its time only: one missed while the server was down is not done when it starts. The pause, each user's limit and the default limit are settings. When the server starts, each setting gets the value of whichever of its changes came last (at or before now), so a server that was down at 20:00 still has the night's value. If two changes of one setting were both missed, only the later one is applied. Adding, editing and deleting changes is audited, and so is every change made. A run that found the value already set is not recorded. The audit reads, for example, scheduled: Claude Code turns at once → 4 (was 1).

docs.title: Sandbox
docs.text: Every run is sandboxed unless a loop's Settings › Preferences › Advanced (admins) says otherwise. The network is open, or an allowlist of hosts, domains and address ranges; HTTP(S) goes through the server's proxy, and raw TCP/UDP is a per-loop choice. The command line's equivalents are FLUX_SANDBOX_NET=allowlist, FLUX_SANDBOX_ALLOW and FLUX_SANDBOX_RAW_NETWORK=1 (Sandbox).

docs.title: Allowlists
docs.text:
Every allowlist (the sandbox's, Chat's, a loop's extra hosts, an agent's hosts and FLUX_SANDBOX_ALLOW) reads the same way:

Entry Allows dl.acm.org that host only *.acm.org or .acm.org acm.org and every subdomain (dl.acm.org, www.acm.org, a.b.acm.org) 10.0.0.0/8, 192.168.1.20, ::1 the addresses in the range, or that address localhost this machine (127.0.0.1, ::1)
  • Separate entries by new lines, commas, semicolons or spaces. # starts a comment to the end of the line.
  • Case, a trailing dot and a port do not count (DL.ACM.org.:443 is dl.acm.org); a pasted URL keeps its host.
  • * alone is refused: choose open (or Chat's Open) instead.
  • Saved, the list is kept one entry per line, and the page says how it reads, for example Understood as: acm.org and its subdomains · arxiv.org only.
  • A page that redirects to another domain (a sign-in or a CDN host) is refused by that host's name. Recently blocked under the list names the hosts refused lately; a click adds one. The agent's error says the same: flux sandbox: refused www.acm.org (not on the network allowlist -- add www.acm.org or *.acm.org).
  • Lists kept before this rule, when a name also allowed its subdomains, were rewritten once as *.name, so they reach what they reached.

Limits restrict every sandbox the server starts: a loop's runs and checks, a loop's Chat, Chat answers, the author agent, agent Tests and logins. For CPUs, memory, processes and scratch /tmp:

  • Default is what a sandbox gets when its loop sets none.
  • Maximum is the most a loop may ask for. A higher ask is clamped to it, never refused, and a loop that sets nothing is held to it too. The run's log says memory 8g clamped to 1g by the server.
  • Empty is no limit (processes: 4096).

CPUs are a positive number such as 2 or 0.5, at most this machine's count. Memory and scratch are sizes with a unit, such as 512m or 4g; memory is at most this machine's RAM. The page shows both. A change is audited (sandbox limits). It applies to sandboxes started after it; running ones keep their limits. A loop's Advanced (admins) shows the server's default and maximum under each field, and clamped to 1g by the server when its value is above the maximum. On a server started with --no-sandbox, the limits are shown read only.

docs.title: Proxy
docs.text:
Proxy is what runs, agents, Chat, logins and the author agent reach the network through, and Flux's own calls to the model endpoints. It applies with or without the sandbox.

  • From the host (the default) takes the first place that names one: the server's environment, /etc/environment, /etc/environment.d/*.conf and ~/.config/environment.d/*.conf, then what the server user's login shell exports (a systemd service often has none of a profile's). The page says which, for example From /etc/environment: HTTP http://proxy:3128 · not for .corp.example.org.
  • Set here takes an HTTP proxy, an HTTPS proxy (each http://host:port, with user:password@ if it asks) and a not through it list, read like an allowlist (new lines, commas, semicolons or spaces; # comments): a host, .domain or *.domain (it and its subdomains), an IP or a CIDR. Empty fields are no proxy. Switching to set here starts from the host's values.
  • Credentials are stored encrypted and shown as http://***@proxy:3128; a URL left as shown keeps them. They never appear on a command line: a sandbox gets them in its variables file.
  • The server and an open sandbox get HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY in both cases, localhost, 127.0.0.1 and ::1 always added to NO_PROXY. An allowlisted sandbox keeps its own proxy (localhost only in its NO_PROXY), which reaches allowed hosts through this one, directly for those its not through it list names.
  • In effect says the proxy and where it came from. A change is audited (sandbox proxy, the credentials masked) and applies to what starts after it: running loops keep theirs.

docs.title: Chat
docs.text:
Admin › Chat says what users may use in Chat. The admin allows features; each user then switches them on or off per chat, within what is allowed.

Feature Allowed Default Chat tab The user has Chat in the top bar. Off, every other feature is off too. on Network beyond the base allowlist A chat may also reach the hosts listed under Network beyond the base allowlist, or any host when it is Open. off Workbench A chat may read and write the user's workbench. on Loop access A chat may read the user's loops, their own and those shared with them, read-only. on
  • For everyone sets the server's value. Overrides sets a value per group and per user: as above, on or off. A user's value beats their groups', which beat the server's; of a user's groups, one that turns a feature off wins. Add a user adds a user's row.
  • A chat always has the sandbox's base allowlist (Sandbox): the hosts listed there, the agents' hosts and the model endpoints. Agents need it, so there is no "off". Allowed with no hosts listed and not Open, the feature stays off, and users see why. On a server whose sandbox network is open, chats have the open network.
  • The hosts beyond the base are an allowlist (Allowlists): *.acm.org lets a chat reach acm.org and all its subdomains. Recently blocked names the hosts chats were refused lately.
  • A feature that is off is greyed in the user's chat, with the reason: turned off by the admin on this server, for the group …, or for you.
  • Changes apply from each chat's next message. They are audited (chat permissions), as are chats made and deleted (chat created, chat deleted).

Limits per answer bound a coding agent's answer: Minutes (default 8, 1 to 60) and Tool calls (default 40, 5 to 400). An answer ends sooner when it is done: once the agent has written its answer (or its question) and then goes quiet, repeats itself, or only updates its plan. An answer stopped at a limit keeps what the agent wrote; with nothing written it fails, saying which limit it reached. FluxAgent has no such limit: it reads with its tools (at most 20 rounds of calls) and then answers.

Attached files bound the files a user attaches to a message, in Chat and in a loop's Chat: MB a file (default 50, 1 to 2048) and Files a message (default 10, 1 to 50). Any type is kept as it is: in the user's workbench (uploads/) or with the answer (Chat › Attached files).

How Think starts in each composer is each agent's and FluxAgent's own: thinking by default, in Admin › Agents. (A server where Chat's earlier Think on by default was ticked has FluxAgent thinking by default.)

Each answer runs as a loop's Chat answers do: in the sandbox, under the server's limits, with the user's model and agent settings, and the agents offered for Ask (Admin › Agents).

Sandbox sets how long a user's chat sandbox is kept idle (minutes, default 30, 0 to 240). A user's answers run in one sandbox, started by their first message and kept between messages, so the next answer starts sooner (about a second instead of two on an idle server); it ends once no answer has run in it for this long. Several chats of the user share it, and so do answers written at the same time, under one set of limits. What an agent keeps between answers is in the user's home and workbench, as before, never only in the sandbox. 0 gives each answer a sandbox of its own.

A sandbox is started again when what it is started with changes: these settings (the network beyond the base, its hosts), the sandbox's (limits, network, PATH, the proxy), the agents' and the model's settings, and, when the server restarts, Flux's code or the server's environment. An answer running at that moment is stopped and written again on the new ones, its message kept and one answer kept, saying restarted: the admin changed the chat settings (or the sandbox settings, the proxy, the agents' settings) or restarted: Flux was updated. One the user may no longer have answered ends stopped, saying why. A finished answer is never touched; the next one simply starts on the new settings. The limits per answer and this time apply from the next answer and start nothing again.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variables apply in order: the server's (Admin › Agents › All agents), the user's (Account), the loop's (Settings › Preferences). Secrets are stored encrypted. The sandbox's own variables, PATH, HOME and the model settings cannot be set this way.

docs.title: Chat
docs.text: Chat, in the top bar, is a conversation with an agent or FluxAgent that belongs to no loop. Ask it about your loops, a paper, an idea; let it write a script or keep notes for next time. It is there when an admin gives it to you (Admin › Chat).

docs.title: The page
docs.text:
Your chats are in a slim rail at the left and the open conversation is in the middle. The Settings panel opens at the right from the Settings button at the top right.

  • New chat starts one. The rail groups chats under Today, This week and Older. A chat whose answer is still being written shows a spinner. ✕ hides the rail and ☰ brings it back.
  • A chat's ⋯ menu, shown on hover and for the open chat, has Rename… and Delete…. Deleting removes its messages and answers; the workbench stays.
  • Open any chat to go on with it: each answer reads the conversation before it.

Your messages are on the right and answers under them. Under each answer one line names the agent and how long it took, and Thinking & commands shows how the answer was made, as in a loop's Chat. When an answer writes or changes files in the workbench, they are listed under it (↳ designs/adder8_csel4.sv). Click one to open it in the panel.

The message box stays at the bottom. Enter sends and Shift+Enter starts a new line (Ctrl+Enter and ⌘+Enter send too). The agent is picked inside the box, from the agents offered for Ask, with your own agent settings (Models and agents). A small ! beside it means the agent is not ready (its connection untested, failed, or changed since its test); click it for Test and Set up.

Think, beside the agent, asks for a slower, more considered answer: FluxAgent reasons before it answers, its thinking shown live in Thinking & commands; a coding agent works at its effort for thinking, and off, at its effort for not (by default its own, and its kind's lowest: Claude Code --effort low, Codex model_reasoning_effort="minimal", OpenCode --variant minimal). Think follows the agent picker: each agent starts as the admin set it (thinking by default) -- every agent on, FluxAgent off unless said -- and your browser remembers your own choice for each agent. A loop's Chat has the same switch. A thinking model that answers nothing is asked again without thinking.

While Think is on, Effort beside it picks how hard a coding agent reasons for this message: the levels its kind takes (Claude Code low to max, Codex and OpenCode minimal to their top; an agent added under a name of its own by its kind), default its effort for thinking. It is sent with the message (flux chat|consult --effort), comes first -- before Think, the loop's box and the admin's default -- and your browser remembers it per agent.

FluxAgent has an Effort too, shown whether Think is on or not: one dial over its thinking, its tool rounds and the length of its answer. default is its effort for Think as set (Admin › Agents: built in medium not thinking -- the answer as before -- and high thinking).

Effort Thinks Tool rounds Answer up to (tokens) Also low no 6 3000 medium no 20 6000 high yes 30 10000 max yes 50 16000 re-reads its draft against the question and what its tools found, and fixes what they do not back (one more call)

Thinking, it asks for the matching reasoning level (reasoning_effort low, medium or high; high at max) where the endpoint takes levels -- asked once per endpoint and model, and left out where refused.

docs.title: Attached files
docs.text:
Attach files to a message with the paperclip beside the agent, by dropping them on the conversation, or by pasting (a screenshot too, named pasted--.png). Each is sent at once: a chip above the box shows its name and size (its progress while it goes), and ✕ removes it. The files go with your next message and show as chips under it; click one to open it (a text highlighted, a picture shown) or download it. Any type is kept as it is. The admin sets the largest file and how many go with one message, 50 MB and 10 unless set otherwise (Admin › Chat).

Where they are kept: with the chat's workbench on, in the workbench's uploads/ (kept across your chats, listed under Settings › Workbench); with it off, with the answer, in its folder's attached/. A name already taken gets a number, notes (2).md: nothing is overwritten.

The answer's brief lists them where its answerer reads them. A coding agent opens them with its own tools (/workbench/uploads/... in its sandbox), pictures too where it reads images. Flux's own model reads a text file as it is, and a document as its text: a PDF through pdftotext (when the server has poppler), Word, Excel, PowerPoint and OpenDocument files directly. The first part of each text is in its brief and read_file reads the rest. It cannot see a picture or read another binary file; its brief says so, and it says so too when the answer depends on one.

In a loop's Chat (the loop's page, or a loop chat here) files attach the same way, for whoever may ask about the loop. They wait in your own folder until the question is sent, then live with its answer, never in the loop's own folders. To put a file in the loop's library, use the loop's Files upload, or accept a chat's proposal.

A coding agent's answer has limits of its own, 8 minutes and 40 tool calls unless the admin set others (Admin › Chat), and it ends as soon as the agent has written its answer and goes quiet, repeats itself or only updates its plan.

Your answers run in a sandbox of your own, kept between messages for a while (30 minutes unless the admin set otherwise, Admin › Chat): the next answer starts sooner. When the admin changes what it runs with, or Flux is updated, an answer being written is written again on the new settings; its row says restarted: … and why, your message is not sent twice.

One answer is written at a time in a chat. Your message shows at once (Sending…). While the answer starts, the row says what is starting: Starting the sandbox…, Preparing the brief…, then Starting OpenCode… (the agent's name). That takes a few seconds, more on a busy server, and is never an error. Once the agent works, the row shows what it is doing now (its latest command, or thinking…) with Stop. Only an answer that ended without answering shows a red notice. An answer stopped after the agent wrote it is kept, marked Stopped before it ended, with its question if it asked one. An answer that fails says why (a rate limit, say) with Ask again, which sends the same message again, to the same agent. When you open a chat, the box starts with the agent of its last answer.

docs.title: Loop chats
docs.text:
Under your chats, the rail folds Loop chats: the conversations held in each loop's own Chat panel, for every loop you can read (yours and those shared with you), one fold per loop that has any. A fold lists the loop's conversations newest first, each titled by its first question, with a count when it has several messages. Whether Loop chats and each loop's fold are open is remembered by this browser.

  • Click a conversation to open it in the middle, with the loop's name as a small tag in its head. It reads as a chat does: Thinking & commands under each answer, Stop while one is being written, and the loop agent's open question on its card while the loop runs. Write in the box to continue it. The answer comes from the loop's own Chat, so the same rules apply: one answer at a time per loop, an agent that reads the loop and changes nothing, and only people allowed to ask about the loop can ask there. Someone you shared the loop with without Ask can read its conversations but not ask, and a conversation asked privately (by someone who may not edit the loop) is shown only to them.
  • Open in NAME opens the loop's page with its Chat panel on that conversation.
  • + New chat on NAME, last in a loop's fold, starts a conversation on that loop. + Chat on another loop does the same for a loop with no conversations yet.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Most answers ask nothing. An agent asks only when it cannot go on without your choice or a value only you know, never to offer more help or to ask permission (a "Would you like me to…?" after a long answer is dropped, and the turn's log says so; so is a question that only says your message back, or asks again what you just answered). The question then ends the answer, shown as a card under it. An answer may ask up to four questions at once; each has a short header, and the headers are chips at the top of the card (✓ Type · Widths · Target, 2 of 3) that move between them. Each question shows

  • its options, one per line: a label, a line on what it means, and Recommended on the one the agent would pick (listed first); pick one, or any for a question that takes several;
  • named values it needs, such as a width or a library, as text, number or list fields;
  • Other, for anything else in your own words (for a free question, the only box).

1–8 pick an option and Enter goes on from anywhere in the card: to the next question, then Send. Next › and Back move too. Send stays off until something is answered; in a card of several, a question left blank is the agent's to decide. You decide lets the agent choose them all and say what it chose.

Your answer goes as one message, to the agent that asked (whichever agent is picked in the box), written plainly, a block per question:

Answer to: Which adder families should adder16's generator try?
- choice: carry-select
- choice: Kogge-Stone

Answer to: Which cell library?
- choice: sky130
keep it small

Your message then shows the answers as chips (Families carry-select, Library sky130), and the card shrinks to what was asked. A chat waiting on your answer is marked ? in the rail. Typing a message in the box instead also answers the question.

A coding agent asks by writing question.json in its folder; FluxAgent ends its answer with a fenced question block, which is taken out of the answer. Either way the questions are

{"questions": [{"header": "Width", "question": "...", "kind": "one" | "many" | "text",
                "options": [{"label": "...", "detail": "...", "recommended": true}],
                "fields": [{"name", "label", "type": "text" | "number" | "choice", "options"}]}],
 "why": "..."}

with at most 4 questions, 8 options and 5 fields each. One question alone, {"question", "kind", "options": ["..."], "fields", "why"}, is read too. Claude Code may ask with its own AskUserQuestion tool instead: when its turn calls it, the call becomes the card (its options' descriptions their detail lines) and the turn ends there.

The server checks every question: one longer than 200 characters asks with its last asking sentence (the rest becomes its reason), an "Other" option is dropped (the card has its own box), and one that is malformed is shown as its text, with a box for a free answer. After You decide, the next answer reads that you delegated the choice, and decides.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
An agent never changes your loops itself: in its sandbox they are read-only. When you ask for a change, or one clearly helps, it proposes it, and each proposal is a card under the answer: what it does and in which loop, why, and a preview. Accept makes it, as you, with the same checks and the same audit trail as the page that does it by hand; Reject drops it. Each proposal is answered on its own; nothing is made without your click. The card then says Done (and what was done), Rejected, or Refused with why. The next answer reads what became of each proposal.

Kind What it does Its preview Library copies files from your workbench into the loop's library/ (papers, notes its agents read) each file, its size and where it goes; replaces when it overwrites one Document writes a text file (.md, .txt, .rst) under the loop's library/, where its agents read it; a lesson (what a run taught) goes under library/lessons/ the text, or the change to the file it replaces Note sends a note to the running loop, as its Notes box does the note Hidden from AI hides paths from the loop's agents, or shows them again (Hidden from AI) the hidden paths before and after Idea adds an idea to the loop's notebook its title, hypothesis and test Queue queues an idea for testing, or takes it off the queue the idea and its place in line Merge ideas merges ideas that say the same thing, as the notebook's cleanup does (it can be undone) the idea kept and those merged into it Design note pins a note on a design, shown in Results' design detail and in Live's inspector the design, its numbers, the note Reference marks a design as a reference for comparison the design and its numbers Settings changes settings of the loop's problem document -- its budget, who works a box, its model, anything the Configure page sets -- saved as the Configure page saves each setting now and proposed; when it takes effect Problem document replaces the text of the loop's problem document (its flow, checks, measurements), saved as Direct edit saves the change, line by line; when it takes effect Measure again measures a design again (a flaky timeout, a tool that failed), as Results' Reject with Measure again does the design, its numbers, the stages, and when it is measured

A note on a design and a reference are for reading only: the loop's decisions, its baseline and its search do not change. A loop reads its problem document when it starts: a Settings or Problem document change reaches a running loop at its next start (Restart starts it again after the pass it is on), and the card says so. Either is proposed only when the document would still load (as Check and flux task check load it); one that would not is refused with the loader's words, and one proposed on a document changed since is refused on Accept, nothing written. Saving settings drops the document's comments, as the Configure page's save does. Until a design is measured again its numbers count as rejected: shown, never chosen; a running loop measures it before its next pass, a loop at rest starts a run of its own. Files the agent brings (a paper it downloaded) go to your workbench first, and the proposal names them there.

The server checks every proposal, when the answer ends and again when you accept it: a loop you own or one shared with you with Edit, not archived. A loop you may only view or ask about gets no proposals at all: the agent is told which loops it may change, and anything it proposes for another is dropped, never shown. Then, the files in your workbench and at most 64 MB each, never an overwrite unless the proposal says so, the problem document only as Settings or Problem document. A coding agent proposes by writing actions.json in its folder; FluxAgent ends its answer with a fenced actions block, which is taken out of the answer. Either way a list of at most 10:

[{"kind": "library.add", "loop": "bob/adder8", "files": ["papers/fast-adders.pdf"], "why": "..."},
 {"kind": "idea.add", "loop": "bob/adder8", "title": "...", "hypothesis": "...", "test": "..."},
 {"kind": "loop.settings", "loop": "bob/adder8", "set": {"budget.passes": 3}, "why": "..."},
 {"kind": "design.recheck", "loop": "bob/adder8", "design": "adder8#3", "why": "its fmax read a timeout"}]

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The panel's Uses says what this chat's answers may use:

Switch On Loops The agent may read your loops: your own, and those shared with you with Ask. The line says how many. Workbench The agent may read and write your workbench. Network The agent may reach the hosts the admin allows for chat, or any host when the admin opens it. Off, it has the sandbox's base allowlist only, which agents need to work. The line says which.

A switch the admin keeps off is greyed, and its line says why. Make these my defaults has new chats start with the current switches. Each answer uses the switches as they were when you sent the message.

In focus (with Loops on) picks one loop from a list you can search, with your loops under Yours and the others under Shared with you. Its record is copied for the answer. FluxAgent asks it with its flux_loop commands first, and queries the copy with the same read-only sql tool as in a loop's Chat only for what no command can say. FluxAgent has no web tool. A coding agent uses its own web tools, within the network the chat allows.

FluxAgent reads no files. With no loop in focus it sees each of your loops' records in a few lines (its objective, how many passes and measurements, its baseline, the best design at each stage and the first objective against the baseline, its last decision), and when an answer needs more it says so and suggests putting that loop in focus. The loop in focus comes with its baseline and how far the best design and the standing pick are from it, objective by objective.

Under Uses is the workbench (see below).

The panel is closed until you open it with the button at the top right (the loop in focus · Settings), and it stays open or closed as you last left it in this browser. Opening a file an answer wrote opens it too. On a wide screen it sits beside the conversation; narrower than about 1360 px it opens over the conversation. On a phone the conversation fills the screen, ☰ opens the chats, and the panel takes the whole screen.

docs.title: Your loops, read-only
docs.text:
With Loops on, every loop you may read is mounted read-only in the answer's sandbox, at /loops/<owner>/<loop>. That includes archived loops and loops shared with you with Ask (a loop you may only view is not there). Another user's loop is never there unless it is shared with you, even for an admin. Each loop's folder has its document, its record and results (out/), its log (runs/loop.log) and its workbench. LOOPS.md, in the answer's folder, lists them with these paths. A coding agent reads a loop with Flux's own read-only commands first -- flux loop summary --loop <its document> (the baseline, the best per objective and the standing pick against it), passes, results, compare, tried, show NAME, events, ideas, notes -- and queries the SQLite record itself last, only for what no command can say.

The questions people ask most are each one command. results ranks the designs at a stage with every metric, a dictionary metric's cases as metric.case (--metrics sim_lost keeps a metric and its cases); --by sim_lost_w ranks by one metric alone; --goals keeps the designs that meet every limit, --stage all shows each design at every stage it reached, --match swizzle keeps those whose text, idea or rationale says the word. compare #6 #12 puts designs side by side, metric by metric, the best on each objective marked. tried --gate consistent lists the designs a stage or a check stopped, with why. events --kind decision reads the record's decisions, conclusions and notes; without --kind it counts each kind.

FluxAgent, which runs no shell, has these as tools: flux_loop runs the same read-only commands on a loop of this chat (summary, passes, results, compare, tried, show, events, design, diff, ideas, notes, library, digest, with the same filters), and list_files and read_file read the loops' folders, the workbench (read-only for it) and the answer's own folder -- nothing else: a path that leads elsewhere, through a link too, is refused, and so is a file a loop hides from AI (Hidden from AI) and another person's conversation about a loop. With a loop in focus it also queries that loop's record (sql), last: its brief and its tools say the commands first. Each query it ran is kept in the answer's folder (sql.jsonl), and asking the same query twice in one answer is not run again. Each call and what came back is in Thinking & commands. A loop's Chat gives FluxAgent the same tools on that one loop.

docs.title: The workbench
docs.text:
The workbench is one folder for all your chats. Agents keep their tools in tools/, notes in notes/ and drafts in drafts/, so a later chat can use what an earlier one made. Chat does not create or run loops: a loop starts from New loop, and a draft for one (a document, a generator) waits in drafts/. In the sandbox it is /workbench; nothing else outside the answer's own folder is writable.

The panel's Workbench shows it as a tree: a folder opens in place, and a file opens in place of the tree, read-only, with Download, Delete and ⛶ Fullscreen. A text is highlighted as in Files, and a picture (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, SVG) is shown. ‹ Workbench goes back. Refresh reads it again; it is also read again when an answer ends. Each answer records the workbench files it wrote: those its agent's writing steps name, and any other file made or changed while it ran. When another of your chats was answering at the same time, a file no step of this answer names may be the other's: it is dimmed, changed meanwhile.

docs.title: Where it is kept
docs.text: On the server, under users/<you>/chat/: workbench/, and chats/<id>/ for each chat; files attached but not sent yet wait in pending/, outside the folders a sandbox mounts. Your chat sandbox has the chats/ folder at /chats and the workbench at /workbench: an answer's agent can read and write your other chats' folders as well as its own. So nothing the server acts on is taken from there: which process Stop ends, or a restart starts again, is the server's own record of what it launched (kept outside every sandbox, each process checked by its start time), never the pid a message's turn.json shows. A chat's folder holds its name, its switches and one folder per message: the message, the answer, the agent's turn, its log, the files attached to it (attached/, and attached.json naming each one, those in the workbench's uploads/ too), the workbench files it wrote, the question it asked and its proposals with what became of them. Creating and deleting a chat is in the audit trail, and so is each accepted proposal (from chat).

docs.title: Files
docs.text: A loop's Files tab shows its folder four ways, each a view in the row under the tabs with its count: Workbench, Library, Inputs and All files. Every file of the loop is in one of the first three, or in what they leave out: out/ and runs/ (what runs write), the document (its place is Settings › Problem) and what All files hides unless asked. On a phone each view lists first; a file opens on its own, with ‹ Back to the list.

docs.title: Workbench
docs.text: The agents' own folder, workbench/: a search over names and first lines, then Overview (the setup's workbench/README.md, opened first when there is one), Tools (five shown, then "N more"), the notes by age (Today, Yesterday, This week, and Older folded with its count), Numbered notes -- notes named one name and a number (draft1297-…, orch-pass12-…), three or more of a name, folded into one row with their count and the newest's age -- and Other for the rest. Each row is a file's name, its age and its first line; it opens in the same viewer as All files (edit, save, download, Actions).

docs.title: Library
docs.text:
What the agents read: the loop's own library/, one row a document (its kind -- PDF, MD, SRC for a folder of source code -- its title, its pages, lines or files), ✓ digested once the setup's model has digested it, not relevant when its digest says it does not bear on the problem. N of M digested sums it up; a search filters the list; ↻ reads it again and {} shows the digests as recorded. + Add a document opens the uploader: files and folders dropped or chosen go into library/. Each project library the loop reads (library/<project>@<group>/) follows as its own group, read-only, Library › opening the project's Library tab. Digests of files outside the library (the loop's notes, its knowledge files) are listed under Also digested.

Open a document and it shows beside the list: what it is, Download and Raw, Actions on your own, then its Digest (the text the prompts read, who made it, how much it read, from where) and its Outline -- its sections with their pages or lines, read as flux library outline reads them (a PDF needs pdftotext on the server; without it the outline says so). A folder shows its files.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Everything else the loop was given: In the problem -- the files and folders the document names beside it (its golden model, the files of its commands, its knowledge sheet and files, its sub-loops), as the loop's own check reads them -- then Skills (a skills/ folder, or the one the document's skills names) and Other. A folder whose files all belong to one group is one row; a lock marks what is hidden from AI. Its foot names the document and links Settings › Problem.

docs.title: All files
docs.text:
The folder as it is: the document, your scripts, library/, the workbench and what Flux writes (out/, runs/). Open a file to view, edit, save or download it; Raw and Fullscreen show the whole of it. Drop files or folders onto the list, or use Add files and Add folder.

  • Actions on a file or folder: Rename…, Move…, Delete…, and Hide from AI (or Show to AI), which adds the path to knowledge.hidden (Knowledge, skills, hidden paths).
  • A name with @ at the top of library/ is refused (when adding, renaming or moving): that is where a project's library appears, library/<project>@<group>/.
  • Under library/, after the loop's own folders, each project the loop is linked into shows its library, in the loop's project order, marked project · read-only (a link to the project's Library tab): browse and download it here, change it on the project's page. The loop's agents read it there with flux library (its own files and the projects', by name, in capped pieces: Reading the library), the project's hidden paths hidden from them too. You see the projects whose link you see (a global project's only to its owner, admins and the project's keepers), and open those whose library you view.
  • The loop's .gitignore files hide what they ignore; show ignored lists them greyed.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: A loop's Settings has two parts, Preferences and Problem.

docs.title: Preferences
docs.text:
• Measurements: per metric, whether it is shown, whether it is a main one (in lists and summaries), and whether it shows as change from the baseline. Charts and the decision always use every measurement.
  • Environment variables: the loop's own, over your account's and the server's.
  • Sharing: the member grid of groups and projects (the words): the Owner row fixed on top, then a row a user or a group shared with, a Level (Viewer, Asker, Contributor, Maintainer; Custom a mix) and a box per word: view (runs, log, results, files; always on), ask (ask an agent about it in its Chat; a chat's agent reads it), edit (its files, the document, its settings, notes; accept Chat's proposals for it), run (start, stop, restart, measure again) and share (this list); there is no Member column on a loop, view is what being shared gives. + Share with… under the grid searches the users and groups and adds the one picked as a Viewer; its level menu or boxes give the rest. Ticking a box saves the row; one with share who is not the owner gives at most what they hold (hover a word's column for its meaning). Edit without Run changes the loop but cannot start or stop it; Ask without Edit chats about it and changes nothing. Under the shares, a read-only row per project the loop is linked into (its title, a project badge, its address as a link) ticks the most any of its people gets on the loop; a global project "gives no rights". ▸ unrolls its people: each member (the words their level gives), a member of its group who gets more through their membership ("via group"), and one row for what its group access gives everyone in the group ("Everyone in hw · open (Asker+)"); Change on the project › opens its page, where they are set. Your rights on a loop are your row, your groups' rows and what its projects give you, together; being in a group with its owner gives nothing. A run started by someone else uses the owner's record, model settings and limits.
  • Projects: the projects the loop is linked into, in its order: a grip to drag a row, or ▲ ▼ (the order its projects' libraries come in, each read-only at library/<project>@<group>/ after the loop's own files; an exact copy of a paper in a later one is read once). Each row has the project and its address, learns from runs (whether the project may learn from its runs) and ✕ to take it out. Add to a project… searches the projects you may link it into: those where you hold the link role, and the global ones that take loops. Linking it is your consent: each of the project's members gets their loop words on it (view, ask, edit, run; never share), and the group's members what its access gives. A global project gives no rights; its learning is off until an admin or one of its managers turns it on, and you may turn it off. Others see the card read-only.
  • Name & ownership: rename the loop (1 to 60 letters, digits, _ and -), or transfer it to another user. The loop must be stopped, with no agent and no chat answer reading it at work. Everything that names the loop moves with it -- its record, results, runs and settings, chats that focus on it or proposed changes to it, scheduled changes, waiting notices' links, its usage (counted once). There are no redirects: the old address stops working. A transfer leaves the admin's overrides, the shares and the agents' tests behind (they were the old owner's); the log, transcripts and the audit keep the old name where it was written.
  • Advanced (admins): whether the loop runs in the sandbox, its memory, CPU, process and scratch limits (under each, the server's default and maximum; an ask above the maximum is clamped to it, see Sandbox limits), parallel work (how much, the configurator's Extra › Running, which says whether it is allowed), extra hosts it may reach, raw TCP/UDP, host folders mounted inside, and extra Nixpkgs or Nixchip packages. Everyone else sees what they are, in a line under Name & ownership.
  • Maintenance (folded): run a clean-up on this loop now, and Re-Evaluate, which asks the next start to measure the pending designs again -- its boxes add pass 0 (Rerun baseline), the failed designs (Rerun failed) or every design (Rerun all). What waits for the next start is said on its row and on the Overview, with Cancel; it can be asked while the loop runs. Invalidate all sets every design aside without measuring anything; Show hidden evaluations brings back what an older invalidation hid. The tasks that change what the record counts are red and ask first. While an invalidation's designs wait to be measured again, its row says how many are done (Results).
  • Archive, reset or delete: Archive… keeps a finished loop read-only and frees its disk (see Archive). Reset clears what the runs generated (you choose what to keep: the workbench, results and history, caches); the document, your files and the settings stay. Delete removes the whole loop. All need the loop stopped and cannot be undone.

docs.title: Archive
docs.text:
Archive… (the loop's owner, or an admin) asks for the loop's name and lists, with their sizes, what goes and what stays.

Kept Deleted The record, out/: designs, measurements, decisions (Results and its exports) Each pass's agent folders: prompts, drafts, sessions, probes The document, your files and the library The tools' whole outputs (the journal keeps each one's end) The workbench's notes and tools The sandbox's tool caches and scratch The last start's log, the answer, notes and Chat The author's work in progress, __pycache__, the workbench's build folders The task journals and transcripts Live reads The log of the starts before the last; stopped sandbox containers
